### Customizing Character Creation

At each stage of character creation, the default rules have been laid out for three broad Exigent frameworks, but these guidelines are simply the default. A few examples of ways that these rules can be customized are found below:

• Some Exigents may be granted additional specialties to reflect extensive training received after they were Chosen. If they receive more than four specialties, at least two should reflect this training. • Exigents with significant temporal power, such as the Sovereigns of Uluiru (p. XX), may receive an additional five dots of Merits, typically restricted to Story Merits such as Backing, Command, Contacts, Followers, Influence, Resources, and Retainers. Alternatively, these additional dots might be restricted to a particular Merit. For instance, Ninegala, the ForgeGoddess of Makelo, might allow her Chosen to take powerful Artifacts from her vault.

• Many Exigents have unique choices to make during Step 1 that help to define their overall concept, such as an Architect choosing her home city.

• Like the Lunar Exalted, some Attribute-based Exigents may possess superhuman potency. These (typically) Celestial-level Exigents distribute nine dots between primary Attributes,

EX3

### EXIGENTS GET SPECIAL POWERS, TOO

Most types of Exalted have unique powers or advantages that take them above the baseline described in this chapter: Solars’ Supernal Abilities, Dragon-Blooded’s Elemental Aura and access to Resonant Evocations, Lunar shapeshifting and moonsilver tattoos, Sidereals’ arcane fate and astrological powers, and so on. Exigents can have these advantages too, whether it’s a unique power separate from Charms or superior access to Martial Arts, Evocations, or sorcery. If you don’t give your Exigent such an edge, take that into consideration when creating their Charms, making them more powerful in places that let them keep pace with other Exalt’s advantages.

Significant Deviations

What if you want to go further than fine-tuning the rules of character creation in small ways? You could design an Exigent that only possesses Favored Abilities, which strongly reflects how the character’s power is rooted in her personal interests. She might possess fewer than 10 Caste/Favored Abilities, whether because her power is narrowly focused or because you simply can’t think of ten different Abilities which the character has an interest in. An Essence-based Exigent could possess Favored Abilities or Attributes. Or an Essence-based Exigent whose esoteric patron has an affinity for sorcery might receive Favored costs on spells without selecting either Intelligence or Occult as Caste/Favored Traits.

Discuss each of these ideas with your Storyteller and try to find a rationale reflecting the nature and personality of the Exigent you want to play. Your Storyteller should err on the side of generosity, and if you propose an idea that he wants to turn down, he should try to work with you to understand why you feel it’s important, and whether your proposal is necessary.

a spread of Favored Abilities or Favored Attributes. For Ability-based Exigents, a Caste or Aspect typically has five associated Abilities, although if there’s significant overlap among these Abilities (e.g., having multiple combat Abilities), they might be associated with a total of eight, from which the player picks five. For Attributebased Exigents, Castes and Aspects are associated with three Attributes, of which the player may choose two depending on how many Favored Attributes she receives.

### Anima

Each Exigent has an anima banner that flares with greater brightness and intensity as she spends peripheral motes. Every five peripheral motes she spends in an instant increase her anima banner by one level.

Dim

The Exigent’s anima is invisible. This is its default level when she’s not spending Essence.

Glowing

The Exigent’s anima becomes visible,

outlining her body and potentially manifesting other visual displays like Caste Marks, glowing eyes, a halo of power,

etc. Stealth rolls suffer a −3 penalty; other characters add +3 dice on rolls

opposing the Exigent’s disguise.

Burning

The Exigent’s anima coalesces into an

aura surrounding her and may have

cosmetic effects on objects or terrain it touches. Stealth is impossible.

Bonfire/

Iconic

The Exigent’s anima ignites into a brilliant bonfire stretching into the sky, visible for miles around. Upon reaching bonfire and at suitably dramatic moments, her anima manifests a personalized iconic display that reflects both her personality and the nature of her Exaltation. Her anima completely illuminates her surroundings within short range. Stealth is impossible.

## Traits

### Castes and Aspects

Most Exigents are singular Exalted, but some among those who exist in greater numbers have Castes or Aspects. A Caste is fundamentally about what the Exigent does, reflecting a role that the Exigent was chosen to fulfill, like the warrior role of a Dawn Caste Solar or the trickster role of a Changing Moon Caste Lunar. Aspects are about who an Exigent is, reflecting her nature, personality, and talents, like the passionate intensity of a Fire Aspect Dragon-Blood or the choleric temperament of a Flesh Aspect Liminal. A Caste or Aspect is associated with a set of anima effects, a set of criteria for receiving a Role Bonus (p. XX), and

EX3

It takes 15 minutes for the anima banner to recede from bonfire to burning or from burning to glowing, and half an hour to recede from glowing to dim.

Caste or Aspect an anima effect that would be highly desirable for many character concepts supported by other Castes or Aspects.

Anima Effects

Each Exigent has three main anima effects, powers that are iconic of either their Caste or Aspect or, if they don’t have one, their nature as an Exigent. These anima effects function much as Charms do (see Chapter 4, p. XX), but are generally straightforward bonuses rather than the more complex powers that some Charms have. A very common structure for anima effects is a power that provides an Instant-duration benefit for five motes but becomes free at bonfire anima.

In addition to an Exigent’s main anima effects, they may have a number of minor and largely cosmetic powers that can be used for one mote, like a Solar displaying her Caste Mark or knowing the time from the position of celestial bodies.

For Exigents without a Caste or Aspect, their anima effects are universally available regardless of character concept as the most basic manifestations of their power. For Exigents with Castes or Aspects, these anima effects are still universally available to members of that Caste or Aspect, but unlike Charms, they’re completely unavailable to Exalted of other Castes or Aspects — so it’s best to avoid giving a

### Merits and Flaws

Some Exalted have unique Merits or Flaws available to them, reflecting specific aspects of their nature as an Exalt that couldn’t be represented as a Charm. Such Merits are always Innate or Purchased, not Story Merits. For example, Architects have Merits that let them exchange a Foundation Attribute for greater power with Martial Arts or sorcery (p. XX), while the Thin-Blooded Flaw (Dragon-Blooded, p. 143) poses complication to a Dragon-Blood in the unique issue of their Exalted lineage.

EX3

### The Great Curse

The death-curse of the fallen ancients fell upon the fire of the Exigence just as it did the other Exalted, ensuring that all Exigents created from it would bear the mark of their vengeance. The Great Curse manifests differently for each Exigent. For many, the Great Curse’s manifestations function similarly to Solar Limit (Exalted, p. 134): the Exigent has a ten-point Limit track; gains or loses Limit under certain conditions, and upon reaching 10; and enters a Limit Break, a dramatically altered state of mind.

While in Limit Break, the Exigent treats it as a Defining Intimacy and must reject any influence it would let them treat as unacceptable (Exalted, p. 220). Once a Limit Break ends, the Exigent’s Limit resets to zero and her current temporary Willpower resets to an amount equal to her permanent Willpower. The Great Curse can also be represented purely through roleplaying, as with Dragon-Blooded and Architects (p. XX). An Exigent using these rules can earn an Expression Bonus of Exigent Experience (p. XX) through roleplaying manifestations of their Great Curse. However, this is never an excuse to ruin other players’ fun at the table. If a dramatic moment caused by the Great Curse isn’t something that the entire group can appreciate, it doesn’t award Exigent Experience. The choice between these two is a matter of theme and player preference, not power level or balance. You can freely change an Exalt’s Limit track to a purely roleplay-based Great Curse if you prefer it, or vice versa. You can customize these mechanics or create new ones to suit your Exigent. For example, the optional canon Umbral Exalted (p. XX) have a ten-point track of Penumbra that represents their Shadow’s influence over them, but don’t have Limit Breaks; their Penumbra waxes and wanes as they contend with their Shadow.

### Martial Arts

The rule of thumb for which Exalted have access to the Mastery keyword with Martial Arts and which are limited by the Terrestrial keyword varies based on what level of play they’re designed for.

Terrestrial Play

Terrestrial Exigents are generally limited by the Terrestrial keyword when using Martial Arts. Some have ways to circumvent this limitation, like DragonBlooded using the Immaculate styles, while others may

not suffer from it at all if it fits their themes. However, even the most thematically appropriate Terrestrial Exigent generally won’t have Mastery unless you’re willing to design their entire Charm set around them having access to Solar-level Charms in Martial Arts. This is doubly true for Sidereal Martial Arts, whose power, scale, and scope risk overshadowing any other magic a Terrestrial Exigent has access to. Celestial Play

Celestial Exigents are generally never limited by the Terrestrial keyword. It’s not a useful tool for power balance, as players will simply avoid Martial Arts in favor of more powerful magic. Celestial Exigents can have the Mastery keyword if it fits their themes, or may receive Mastery with a limited selection of thematic styles. For instance, the Chosen of a serpentine god might have Mastery with Snake style, White Veil style, and other styles that employ poison. However, keep in mind that this strongly pressures players to use those styles over any others. That’s not a problem if the Exigent is only meant for one player who was planning to take those styles anyway, but for an Exigent designed for a broader audience, it risks shutting down potential character concepts and character-building decisions. Sidereal Martial Arts aren’t off limits for Exigents with appropriate themes. Such Exigents are vanishingly rare in Creation, but they’re fair game for a player character concept. If you want to play one, make sure you aren’t potentially overshadowing another player’s character concept. If someone’s playing a Sidereal or Solar, or similar character with plans to eventually take Sidereal Martial Arts, talk with them and the Storyteller to make sure that won’t be an issue. Limiting an Exigent’s access to a single style or a selection of thematic styles can be a good way to resolve this by giving access to styles the other player doesn’t plan to take. Exigents generally never have access to the Enlightenment keyword, which empowers Sidereal Martial Arts in the hands of Sidereals and Getimians. An Exigent for whom Martial Arts is a core focus might have Enlightenment for a single style that directly matches their themes: the Chosen of a former god of healing whose divine purview was corrupted by the Great Contagion might have Enlightenment with Citrine Poxes of Contagion style, which is about disease and healing.

Martial Arts Compatibility

Because of how Martial Arts compatibility works, Exalted with Ability-based Charms can’t use their combat Abilities’ Charms together with Martial Arts,

EX3

but those with Attribute-based or Essence-based Charms aren’t similarly limited. Likewise, Exigents with Charms for a limited Ability spread (p. XX) can circumvent the restriction if their offensive Charms reside in non-combat Abilities. This is a significant advantage that can risk becoming overpowered without some balancing factor.

For Celestial Exigents, having such compatibility usually means that they don’t have Mastery with Martial Arts, and tend to have more Simple-type offensive Charms than others. Terrestrial Exigents typically lose this compatibility altogether, except for Charms with the Versatile keyword, below.

These are safe approaches, but not the only ones — if, for example, Martial Arts prowess is a significant part of your Terrestrial Exigent’s themes, you could have them keep this compatibility, with the tradeoff being in the overall power level of their native combat Charms. In terms of a “power ceiling” when pushing these limits, Terrestrial Exigents shouldn’t outshine a Dragon-Blooded with an Immaculate style, and Celestial Exigents shouldn’t outshine Solars or Sidereals with Sidereal Martial Arts.

Celestial Play

Celestial Exalted typically have access to Celestial Circle sorcery and Ivory Circle necromancy, or Shadow Circle necromancy and Terrestrial Circle sorcery. Celestial Exigents with appropriate themes might have access to both the Celestial Circle and the Shadow Circle. Some may be worse at sorcery than this for thematic or balance reasons — unlike with Martial Arts and the Terrestrial keyword, a sorcerer can still gain great benefit from Terrestrial Circle spells even if she can’t initiate into the Celestial Circle. Exigents with appropriate themes might be able to initiate into the Solar Circle or Void Circle, or more commonly, gain conditional access to a limited selection of thematically appropriate spells. If someone else is playing a Solar, Abyssal, or Infernal with plans of reaching the third circle, you’ll want to discuss it with them to ensure you’re not stealing their thunder. Even then, an Exigent shouldn’t have access to both the Solar Circle and the Void Circle.

Initiation Charms

Initiation Charms for sorcery and necromancy have the same trait minimums across Exalt types:

Keyword: Versatile

Versatile Charms are always compatible with Martial Arts. Versatile Charms from multiple Abilities or Attributes can’t be used together on the same action, unless specified otherwise. If a Versatile Charm is in a combat Ability or involves a roll or static value using one, its compatibility is limited to Martial Arts that use weapons for that combat Ability.

• Terrestrial Circle/Ivory Circle: Occult 3, Essence 1 for Ability-based Exalted; Intelligence 3, Essence 1 for Attribute-based Exalted; or Essence 1 for Essence-based Exalted.

• Celestial Circle/Shadow Circle: Occult 4, Essence 3 for Ability-based Exalted; Intelligence 4, Essence 3 for Attribute-based Exalted; or Essence 3 for Essence-based Exalted.

### Sorcery and Necromancy

• Solar Circle/Void Circle: Occult 5, Essence 5 for Ability-based Exalted; Intelligence 5, Essence 5 for Attribute-based Exalted; or Essence 5 for Essence-based Exalted.

An Exalt’s access to sorcery and necromancy varies based on the tier of play she’s designed for. Terrestrial Play

Terrestrial Exalted are generally capable of initiating into Terrestrial Circle sorcery or Ivory Circle necromancy. Exigents with appropriate themes may vary from this, like a knowledge-god’s Chosen being able to learn Celestial Circle sorcery as a unique, distinguishing advantage (p. XX). It’s more common for Terrestrial Exigents to gain conditional access to a limited selection of higher-Circle spells, as with Sovereigns’ Sapphire Talisman Apocrypha (p. XX). Exigents whose themes are associated with necromancy may have access to both Terrestrial Circle sorcery and Ivory Circle necromancy, if using both makes sense for their concept.

The minimums for sorcery Charms, on the other hand, vary based both on theme. Solars and other Exalted for whom sorcery or necromancy is core to their themes — even Terrestrial Exigents — need no prerequisite Charms to learn Terrestrial Circle sorcery or Ivory Circle necromancy, and need only the preceding initiation Charms to learn those for higher Circles. All Exalted with access to Solar Circle sorcery or Void Circle necromancy fall into this category. For other Exalted, Terrestrial Circle sorcery and Ivory Circle necromancy generally require either four Charms from some specific category, like “Occult Charms” or “Mental Charms,” or one specific Charm.

EX3

might also have one for certain kinds of artifacts, like the Puppeteer’s resonance with artifact puppets.

### NECROMANCY

Terrestrial Play

Terrestrial Exalted are typically neutral with one of the magical materials and dissonant with all others. As always, the may vary — Dragon-Blooded are masters of Evocations in Terrestrial play, resonant with jade and neutral with all other materials but soulsteel, while Sovereigns can gain resonance with adamant using Adamant Harmony Reverberation (p. XX). Note that resonant Evocations are almost always more powerful than other magic a Terrestrial Exalt can learn. Broad, unconditional access to Evocations like that of the Dragon-Blooded warrants increasing the experience cost of Evocations to twelve points to mitigate the potential for a “one true build” based on resonant Evocations.

The three circles of necromancy are the Ivory Circle, the Shadow Circle, and the Void Circle. While rules for necromancy haven’t yet been presented, for Storytellers wishing to approximate them, necromancers have access to all sorcery spells except for those that have healing or life-nurturing effects, like Benediction of Archgenesis, and summoning spells, like Demon of the First Circle. In exchange, necromancers have access to unique spells dealing with creating, summoning, and manipulating the undead, manipulating or exploiting the nature of the Underworld and shadowlands, laying deathly curses, and other bleak magics. If a sorcerous spell creates or draws on the five elements, its necromantic equivalent will instead manifest phantasmal phenomena of the Underworld — a necromancer casting Flight of the Brilliant Raptor might conjure a bird of the eerie green foxfire that burns in the Underworld’s marshes, rather than true flame. This doesn’t change the spell’s effects.

Celestial Play

Celestial Exigents are usually resonant with one magical material appropriate to their theme and neutral with all others. If thematically appropriate — e.g., for the Chosen of a god of precious metals or artifice — they may be resonant with multiple materials, or even all materials.

Necromancy has its own equivalent to sorcerous workings. They’re largely identical, but necromantic workings are incapable of healing or nurturing life unless they do so by draining vitality from another, and they cannot summon entities other than the undead. In Creation, necromantic workings always cause some degree of backlash to the living and the land around it, although a skillful necromancer can minimize or precisely limit this — or potentially draw greater power from a working by letting its backlash go entirely unrestrained.

### Advancement

Exigents receive five experience points per session. Depending on whether they’re intended for Terrestrial or Celestial play, they default to one of the two tables of experience point costs below. Most Essence-based Exigents pay 9 experience for all Charms, including Martial Arts Charms, spells, and Evocations. Terrestrial Advancement

For the latter, there might be a selection of Charms the Exalt can choose them, if they have multiple Charms that make sense as a foundation for their esoteric initiation. Celestial Circle sorcery and Shadow Circle necromancy require the preceding initiation Charm and any five spells of the preceding circle.

### Evocations

An Exalt’s level of proficiency with Evocations depends on the tier of play she’s designed for. While these are generally based on the five magical materials (or six, including adamant), some Exigents have an affinity for exotic components, like Chiaroscuro glass. ### Exigent Experience

In addition to experience awarded at a session’s end, Exigents have the opportunity to earn Exigent experience, which can be spent to gain any trait (or on any other experience point cost, such as sorcerous workings) except Exigent Charms. Typically, players can earn one Expression Bonus and one Role Bonus per session, each of which grants two

For example, the Bleak Warden’s concept revolves around binding and subduing spirits, as well as a flawless memory. His role bonuses might include successfully tracking down and binding a danger threatening Creation, or when his eidetic memory retains clues that lead him to his target. The Torchbearer, on the other hand, might earn role bonuses by uncovering corruption and revealing it, or inspiring others to pursue knowledge.

## The Nature of Exigence

Beyond the mechanics of creating Exigents, there are a few narrative concerns which can influence their themes and stories described below.

EX3

WHAT’S THE POINT?

Essence fever is a narrative tool to encourage the Exalted to act dramatically. If a person receives phenomenal power, what fun would it be if they simply sat on it and didn’t do anything? Essence fever provides characters, both player- and Storyteller-controlled, an easy rationale for making dramatic (and interesting) changes to their lives. Consider Essence fever an opportunity to figure out how their newfound power might change a character’s behavior from before they were Chosen, and a handy answer for why they might join a Circle of their fellow Exalted as they adventure. Essence fever is not mind control. Rather, it’s a dramatic prompt to help answer a simple question: What’s my motivation?

### Essence Fever

An Exigent’s Essence fever echoes the heady power imparted by the Unconquered Sun, an urge to action that suffuses the divine fire of Exigence and all those created from it. This urge focuses on the circumstances in which an Exigent was chosen. For instance, Strawmaiden Janest feels in every fiber of her being that she must protect her people from annihilation and tend to the fields that Ten Sheaves held so dearly. This impulse doesn’t overcome reason but serves as a powerful impetus to act decisively to address whatever challenges she was chosen to overcome.

This compulsion doesn’t suddenly disappear when the Exigent’s work is accomplished. She continues to feel the burning desire to act and wield her Essence in the world, even when she lacks an easy target. Eager to achieve the highs she felt when she Exalted, she may seek to enact her agenda on a more ambitious scale, or wander Creation in search of another cause — whether similar to or radically different from that for which she was chosen. Regardless of the nature of their power or their personal character, few Exigents resist Essence fever, though some grow more adept at controlling these urges as they age.

EX3

The details of an Exigent’s Essence fever are heavily influenced by the god who catalyzed her Exaltation. An Exigent of the violent war-goddess Siakal may have been Exalted to protect the war-god’s people, but Siakal’s Essence within him calls him to slaughter, staining the Great Western Ocean red in the blood of his enemies. Conversely, an Exigent chosen by the gentle Forest Walker called Ten Wise Branches, when confronted by an angry mob, finds herself struggling with the impulse to force serenity and peace upon these people somehow.

### Exigent Longevity

When designing an Exigent, matters of lifespan may be academic, as chronicles don’t often last long enough for characters to die of old age. Nonetheless, the choice may present an opportunity to give a character a dramatic motivation related to their age. Storytellercontrolled Exigents may bargain for ways to extend their lifespan, while aging Exigents may act to solidify their legacy, particularly if they’re able to pass on their power.

### Exigent Inheritance

Many Exigents live a lengthy yet still mortal lifetime, maintaining their health until their final years. Some find ways to extend their lives beyond their natural span with anagathic drugs purchased from the Guild, sorceries learned from gods and demons, or stranger methods of staving off aging. Others have lifespans measured in centuries, which they can extend further using many of the same methods as their shorter-lived peers.

The typical Exigent is a singular being — her power stays with her through her entire life, then dies with her. A few Exigents pass on their Exaltation to another bearer, although their methods of doing so vary greatly. For instance, a dying Torchbearer passes on her power to a successor — ideally a worthy one! — in the form of her lantern. When Karana’s Puppeteer dies, her power returns to the god as a gossamer filament that he may offer to a potential Chosen. Wicked-Grin Shifune (usually begrudgingly) confers power to the person who takes him on as their familiar.

Rarer still are Exigents with the potential to live for millennia. Of these, relatively few have survived the passage of ages, though a few may yet be found, with long and faded memories of the rise and fall of civilizations. Sometimes this persistence is conditional: An Architect does not age as long as she remains within her home city’s bounds, while an Exigent chosen by the forest deity Ever-Rising Oak is only nigh-ageless so long as the titanic tree she guards still stands.

Inheritance is a useful thing to consider when thinking either about the origin of your Exigent’s power, or what you might want to happen over the course of a chronicle. An Exigent who inherited their power may have come to possess it in a highly unusual way, which can be a great seed for adventure. Inheritance can also be a fitting end for a beloved Exigent character, their power passed on to a worthy successor, or waiting in the hopes for one to find it someday.

EX3

In the Tranquil Elm’s banquet hall, Nimah Fel supped his last.

The Thousand Venoms Mistress had followed him around Nexus for days, planning his demise. The lissome Guild factor had carved a flourishing economic empire throughout the Scavenger Lands and brought in practically sinful returns year after year. Small wonder that one of his fellow Guildsmen wanted him dead. Her client had described the arcane politics of the Guild’s Directorate, but she wasn’t paid to care. She slipped into the kitchen and cheerfully showed the chef her knife. He set down his cleaver, remembering somewhere else he needed to be. In Nexus, it’s often best to simply get out of the way. Soup — delicious, from the smell — bubbled on the stove. The Exigent ladled a serving into an exquisite porcelain bowl and tipped in the contents of her ivory vial. It wouldn’t do to poison all the patrons. As she carried it toward the banquet hall’s door, a shaggy-headed but well-heeled man came through the doorway. She’d seen him before, at Fel’s side at the gambling house, even got close enough to hear his name: Willow Specter.

“Oh. I was looking for...” His eyes narrowed. “Where’s the chef?”

“Needed a break,” she said. But Willow Specter was already in motion, knocking the bowl from her hands. Time to abort. Before the bowl hit the floor, she was sprinting for the back door, with Willow Specter following not far behind.

She whipped an envenomed throwing knife behind her with a practiced motion. The blade flew clean and true — until, mere yards away from Willow Specter’s heart, a shopkeeper leaned over a balcony to shake out a rug. The knife buried itself in carpet; a black stain spreading along the fibers.

Willow Specter cast a horrified glance at the venom as he passed but didn’t slow his pursuit. Ahead, the alley forked. The Thousand Venoms Mistress went left. Glancing back, she saw Willow Specter dart right. She hadn’t been in Nexus for long; he might know a shortcut she didn’t. But he wouldn’t expect her to go up.

She hoisted herself up drainpipes and balconies and made for her nearest safehouse, leaping from rooftop to rooftop. As she dashed across the fourth roof, Willow Specter hauled himself up over a ledge. “Lucky break,” he explained. “I wanted a crow’s eye view.” He closed the distance, dagger drawn. She met him with poison-tipped blades of her own. Her strikes were sharp and calculated; his jabs wild and reckless. She should’ve bested him in short order, yet at every turn he parried — not because he’d anticipated her moves, but because his blade happened to be in the right place at the right time. Eventually, though, his luck ran out. She slipped past his guard, slicing a bicep. The poison worked fast. Pain-wracked, Willow Specter dropped to his knees, jaw agape in a wordless scream. It was distilled from the Thousand Venoms Mistress’ own blood, containing every deadly substance she’d procured over her years as the Chosen of Toxins. His eyes went wide with psychedelic hallucinations as it reached his brain. Tears streamed down his cheeks.

Then his hand flashed out, blindly grabbing for the vials at her belt. His fingers, still clumsy and numb, fumbled one from among the many. The only one that mattered. Before she could knock it away, he’d scrambled back to the roof’s edge, where he unstoppered the antidote and swigged.

She might still have been able to slit his throat in that moment as he shuddered and gasped with relief; perhaps she even should have. But her foe intrigued her, and besides, her client had only paid for Fel’s death, not his bodyguard’s.

Willow Specter rocked back onto his knees, watching her warily as the poison’s effects subsided. “I don’t suppose you’d stay away from Fel if I asked nicely?”

“No,” she said. “I have a job to do.”

“I’ll see you around, then.” He scuttled backwards and plummeted off the side. When she peered over the edge, the Chosen of the Dice was gone.

# Chapter Four: Power of the Exalted

Chapter Four

Power of

the Exalted

The supernatural prowess of the Exalted is depicted through their Charms. The Exigents, the most variable of the Chosen, don’t have a single Charm set like Solars, Dragon-Blooded, or other Exalted. Instead, each type of Exigent has its own unique Charm set. Creating an entirely new Charm set can be a daunting task; this chapter exists to present you with the tools to accomplish it.

bare minimum needed to begin playing. If the player is designing the Charms, she only needs to write those Charms she’s interested in having at the beginning of play; if the Storyteller is writing the Charms, she should consult with the Exigent’s player to see what he’s interested in — there’s no need to write social influence Charms if the Exigent’s player isn’t interested in starting out with them.

## Know Your Audience

The rest of your Exigent’s Charm set can be created over the course of play. When using the standard character advancement rules (p. XX), Exigent player characters will be able to take one new Charm every two sessions. If your game goes all the way to Essence 5 — which not all games do — you’ll need to design, at most, a total of thirty-seven new Charms in addition to the ones you made at character over the course of sixty sessions.

One of the most important considerations in creating an Exigent (or any other homebrew mechanic) is who’s going to use it. If you’re creating an Exigent for yourself or another member of your playgroup, you can narrowly tailor your design to the needs of a single player and collaborate with your Storyteller and fellow players to arrive at a design that everyone will enjoy. If you’re writing for a larger audience, such as something you intend to share online in Exalted fan communities, it’s best to design a broader range of play options, as more players may end up playing your Exigent and want to explore different aspects of their Charm set, and to focus more on mechanical balance, as you won’t be able to directly communicate with everyone in every game using your Exigent.

### Designing for Your Playgroup

### Designing for a Larger Audience

When designing an Exigent to be used by a larger audience, you don’t have the advantages of only needing to write the Charms one player will want to use and stretching out the design process throughout the campaign. There’s no “magic number” of Charms to write for larger consumption, but the following guidelines will help design an Exigent Charm set that can support a variety of character concepts.

Assuming a player character Exigent begins at Essence 1 using the standard character creation rules, you’ll only need to create fifteen to eighteen unique Charms for them to begin playing, depending on how many bonus points they spend on Charms — and potentially fewer than that, if they choose to invest in Evocations, Martial Arts Charms, or sorcery. If you’re creating an Exigent intended to be used just by one player in your group, we strongly recommend that you write only the

### GENERAL APPLICABILITY

While this book’s focus is on the Exigents, the design advice provided in this chapter can be applied to creating new Charms for any of the Exalted, as well as Evocations, Martial Arts, and spells.

## The Art of Balance

Balancing mechanics in a system as complex and exception-based as Exalted is necessarily more of an art than a science. There aren’t precise mathematical rules we can present to ensure that a given Exigent is perfectly balanced in comparison to a Dragon-Blood, a Solar, or another Exigent. This doesn’t mean that balance isn’t important — far from it — but rather, that it’s as much an exercise in communicating with your fellow players (including the Storyteller) as it is in rigorous mechanical design. You can’t achieve perfect mechanical balance, but you can talk with the other people at your table to ensure that everyone is having a positive experience with the custom mechanics you’re using, and to make any changes necessary if someone isn’t.

### Balancing for a Playgroup

Balancing an Exigent Charm set for use within a single group is less mechanically intensive than designing one for broader play, instead placing greater importance on the experience the mechanics create for everyone in the game. Rather than memorizing every entry in every book in Exalted Third Edition, you can focus on the Exalt types and individual Charms chosen by the other players in balancing your Exigent’s Charms to ensure they aren’t underpowered or overpowered in comparison. Likewise, you’ll know if your playgroup’s game is for Celestial play or Terrestrial play (p. XX) and can design your Exigent accordingly. The purpose of balancing mechanics is to provide a positive play experience, and designing for a playgroup means you have a direct line to your fellow players. As long as everyone enjoys it when you use a Charm, it doesn’t matter whether or not it’s balanced in some abstract, objective sense. You have the opportunity to communicate with everyone who’ll be engaging with your mechanics and potentially some preexisting knowledge of what kinds of gameplay they find satisfying, an advantage you never have when you’re writing for an audience broader than your own table. Make the most of that advantage by seeking out input, paying attention to what kind of experiences your Charms

are creating or enabling for them, and being willing to listen to their feedback. Charms designed for a single playgroup never have to be “finished” — you can continually refine them over the course of the game based on experience and feedback.

### Balancing for a Larger Audience

When designing for a larger audience, it becomes more important to clearly define how powerful your Exigent should be, and to compare your Charm set with other effects of a similar power level to ensure that the disparity isn’t too large. Be very clear at the outset about whether your Exigent is intended for Celestial play or Terrestrial play, both to ensure your readers understand this and to help guide your own design decisions. The key to this kind of balancing is being aware of other effects that are similar to the one you’re designing and comparing their relative strengths and drawbacks. Exalted Third Edition is a mechanically expansive game with a tremendous number of individual Charms and similar effects, but you don’t need to memorize every single mechanic. Look to the Charm set that’s closest in rough power level to your intended goal to find the first effect to compare your own design to, and you’ll have already done the majority of what’s necessary. Knowing every single stray Evocation, Merit, and spell that’s remotely like your design may be helpful, but it’s absolutely not necessary. As you design more and more Charms, you’ll become more familiar with what effects already exist that you can use as points of comparison, and it will become easier to find multiple points of reference.

It’s important to distinguish balancing a Charm set from making it identical to another Charm set. If you give an Exigent a Charm set that’s identical to the Solar Charm set, only changing the names, then you’ll have an Exigent who’s perfectly balanced against Solars, but who has nothing unique or distinctive to make players want to play them over a Solar. The best way to create Charms that make your Exigent stand out is with the “top-down” approach to design discussed below (p. XX). Not every Charm needs to be a top-down design, and it’s fine to take Charms directly from other Exalted

EX3

Check-Ins and Tune-Ups

Whether you’re playing an Exigent of your own design or bringing someone else’s work to your playgroup, you should always feel free to check in with how a Charm is working or tune it up to fit your group. This should be a conversation that involves everyone at the table, not just the Storyteller and the Exigent’s player. If something feels off, don’t be afraid to say so. If something feels overpowered, propose an alternative and test it out, whether that means increasing the cost or adding additional requirements. On the other hand, if a Charm isn’t getting much use — if it doesn’t feel fun or comes at too high a cost — it’s completely appropriate to ask for or suggest changes that will make the concept work for you.

### THE CUTTING EDGE

The examples in this chapter are primarily drawn from Solar Charms. We do this to ensure that readers need only the Exalted Third Edition core book to make use of this chapter’s design advice. However, as the game line has progressed, the benefits of experience and hindsight mean that mechanics from later books have more refinement and polish than those in the core book, particularly in the areas of wording and clarity. When looking for points of reference to compare your designs to, we recommend also consulting designs from later books, such as Arms of the Chosen,, Dragon-Blooded

Chosen

Dragon-Blooded,, and Lunars

Lunars..

## Balance and Dice

when they fit your Exigent’s needs, but having exciting and innovative Charms mixed in with them will help excite readers and make them want to play your Exigent.

It’s also important to consider the design of your Charm set as a whole, rather than approaching each individual Charm in a vacuum. Exalted Third Edition emphasizes the interactions of all a character’s Charms over the effect of any single Charm when it comes to gauging a character’s overall strength. If seeing the big picture is difficult at first, it may be helpful to put a finished design aside, wait a few weeks, then come back and reread what you’ve written with a focus on finding what synergies exist within the individual pieces of the whole, and then revise to bring everything in line with the intended level of power. It can also help to have someone else read through your work with fresh eyes, especially if you encourage them to find the most powerful combinations of effects they can. Once you’ve put your work out for general consumption, you can still expand and improve on it. While you don’t have the benefit of being an active participant in every game where your design is being used, you can still gain valuable input from readers who use your designs, either as players or as Storytellers. While you don’t need to accept all the feedback you get, it’s always worth considering it carefully. If all the feedback you’re getting indicates that some part of the design is an issue, take a second look and see if there’s something there you can improve on. It’s best not to take feedback personally — if someone spots a problem, that’s an opportunity to improve, not a personal failing. Like everything else about design, taking feedback is a skill; the more you do it, the better you’ll get.

Dice rolls are the foundation of gameplay, and many Charms interact with them. Understanding the balance considerations and the math at play are key to balancing them.

### Dice Limits

Each Exalt type has a dice limit, the maximum amount of bonus dice or successes from Charms that they can add to a roll or static value. Often, the Attribute and Ability used for the roll or static value in question are used to calculate the dice limit, but variations on this can be used to reinforce an Exigent’s themes. For instance, a Chosen of Mathematics might use (Intelligence + Ability) as their dice limit regardless of the Attribute rolled, while a berserker Exigent might use (higher of Ability or Limit). The limit for increasing static values is half the dice limit, rounded down. In terms of setting an Exigent’s dice limit, the most important factor is the style of play they’re designed for. Exalted intended for Celestial play are typically able to reach a limit of 10 dice, unless having a lower dice limit is used to balance access to powerful non-Charm bonuses, as with Sidereals and target number reduction. 10 dice is the maximum on default dice limits. Exalted intended for Terrestrial level play typically reach a limit of 5 dice and go beyond that in specialized circumstances that reinforce their theme. While Dragon-Blooded only go to 6 dice with specialties, other Exalted designed for Terrestrial play might go higher — even as high as 10 dice — but doing so should be conditional, as with the Architect’s Excellencies (p. XX), and must be considered when designing effects for that Exigent that offer bonuses that don’t count against their dice cap.

EX3

### Excellencies

Excellencies are the most common way of adding bonus dice on rolls. Their core function is the same for all Exalt types: add bonus dice for one mote each, or raise static values for two motes per +1. Some Exalted may have additional benefits included in their Excellencies, like Sidereals’ ability to reduce target numbers. How an Exalt gains access to Excellencies depends on the tier of play they’re designed for (p. XX) and whether their Charm set is Ability-based, Attribute-based, or Essence-based.

Terrestrial Play

Excellencies are more powerful when compared to other Charms at the Terrestrial play level. Accordingly, gaining Excellencies requires more investment than at Celestial play. Terrestrial Exalted receive five free Ability Excellencies or two free Attribute Excellencies at character creation, and must purchase further Excellencies as they do with any other Charm. In Terrestrial play, Essence-based Exalted still use Ability or Attribute Excellencies.

For Terrestrial Exalted with full-Ability Charm sets, the experience investment required to gain Excellencies is offset by adding small, additional benefits to them,

### THE STAMINA AND STRENGTH EXCELLENCIES

Attribute-based Exalted gain special benefits from the Stamina and Strength Excellencies. The Stamina Excellency can be used to raise soak for one mote per point. The Strength Excellency can add dice of raw withering damage for one mote each on attacks with weapons that add Strength to their raw damage. Neither of these benefits can exceed half the Exalt’s dice limit, rounded down down..

Some Essence-based Exalted like the Puppeteer have Excellencies based on Attributes. They don’t gain this benefit from their Stamina and Strength Excellencies — only Attribute-based Exalted get them.

EX3

like with Dragon-Blooded Excellencies. Attribute Excellencies instead offset the experience cost with their greater flexibility and smaller number. Likewise, Essence-based Exalted and Exigents with limited Ability spread Charm sets don’t receive additional effects on their Excellencies, offset by the greater ease and lower experience cost of meeting Ability minimums.

dice that show a certain number increases the expected value of each die by approximately .05 successes — the actual amount is slightly higher, because a rerolled die could in turn be rerolled again. Note that rerolling 1s, and to a lesser extent 2s, is more valuable than rerolling other failure numbers, as some supernatural enemies may have Charms that exploit the 1s and 2s on your roll.

Celestial Play

In Celestial play, Ability-based Exalted gain an Excellency in each Caste, Aspect, or Favored Ability they have at 1+, and in each other Ability they have a Charm for. Exigents using a limited Ability spread must purchase Excellencies for the Abilities not included as though they were any other Charm.

• Roll Twice, Take Highest: Effects that let you make two rolls and take the highest result don’t add a flat amount to the expected value of each die; instead, they increase the total expected value of the roll, with higher dice pools benefitting more. With five dice, rolling twice adds only about .8 successes on average, but at ten dice, it adds about 1.2 successes on average, and at twenty dice, it adds 1.7 successes on average.

Attribute-based Exalted gain an Excellency in each Caste, Aspect, or Favored Attribute they have at 3+ or for which they have a Charm. For other Attributes, they must have it at five or have two Charms to gain its Excellency. Exigents using limited Attribute spreads must purchase Excellencies for other Attributes separately.

• Target Number Manipulation: Lowering a roll’s target number (Exalted, p. 184) increases the expected value of each die by .1 successes per point, while raising the target number decreases the expected value by .1 successes per point. Note that no effect can raise a roll’s target number above 9 (.3 successes per die) or below 4 (.8 successes per die).

Essence-based Exalted in Celestial play don’t use formalized Excellencies — instead, as long as an action or static value uses an Attribute they have at 5 or an Ability they have at 3+, they count as having an Excellency for it. This is just a way to avoid having to keep track of both Attribute and Ability Excellencies on your character sheet.

Dice Tricks and Probability

When designing Charms, it’s important to understand how the probabilities involved in Exalted’s dice rolling system work. On average, a single die will roll a failure 60% of the time. However, because of the double 10s rule that applies to almost all rolls, the expected value of a single die (i.e., the average of all possible results) is .5 successes, rather than .4. For instance, the expected value of rolling ten dice is five successes. While it’s an easy formula to remember, there are a number of effects that can alter the expected value of a dice roll. • Double Successes: Doubling successes (e.g., double 9s, double 8s) increases the expected value of each die by .1 for each doubled number: .6 for double 9s, .7 for double 8s, and .8 for double 7s.

• Rerolling Dice: Rerolling a flat number of failed dice is roughly equivalent to adding that many non-Charm dice to a roll. Rerolling all failed

• Inflicting Penalties: Each point of penalty inflicted on an opposing roll is roughly equivalent to one non-Charm die added to your own roll. • No Double 10s: Removing double 10s, which primarily occurs on decisive damage rolls, reduces the expected value of each die to .4 successes.

Automatic successes don’t have any synergy with most dice tricks.

### Non-Charm Dice and Systems

Doubling 7s on a Bureaucracy roll to know local currency exchange rates is a very different thing than doubling 7s on a decisive attack roll to dispatch a wrathful Exalt. Exalted’s various systems call for different approaches in terms of how many non-Charm dice they can add — either directly, or effectively through dice tricks. The following guidelines are a bird’s-eye overview; gauging the specifics is a matter of comparing existing Charms. Attack rolls and Defense values receive the least in terms of non-Charm bonuses, as too high a bonus on

### DICE LIMITS AND THE UN-EXALTED

Many Charms allow one character to add bonuses to a roll made by another. This isn’t a problem when that other character is Exalted — they all have their own intrinsic limits on how many bonus dice they can add to a roll. This isn’t the case when it comes to mortal allies, animal familiars, summoned demons, or the countless other un-Exalted characters in Creation. Some powerful supernatural beings, like the war-god Ahlat (Exalted, p. 514) and the demon Octavian (Exalted, p. 530) have their own magic that’s capable of adding dice or automatic successes to their rolls. For such characters, you can apply whatever limit those Charms specify to any magic that adds bonuses to those character’s rolls. If a single Charm provides a benefit that exceeds a character’s recommended dice limit, it’s fine to let it take precedence — the main purpose of dice limits is to restrict the power of combinations of effects. Likewise, it’s fine to ignore the guidelines where it’s clear that a group of Charms is written with the intent that all of them can be used together to enhance a character — for example, the Solar Presence Charms Empowering Shout (Exalted, p. 370) and Favor-Conferring Prana (Exalted, p. 374).

Social rolls have more room for non-Charm bonuses, as the social influence system provides a safety net for characters beaten by influence rolls in the form of resisting with Willpower and unacceptable influence. The same is true for various opposed rolls — Awareness vs. Stealth, Investigation vs. Larceny, War vs. War, etc. The highest non-Charm bonuses are typically only applicable to actions rolled against a flat difficulty, like feats of strength, introduce fact rolls, and many Medicine rolls. Without an opposing character contesting a roll, the consequences of failure may be less interesting than the consequences of success. The crafting and sorcerous working systems are unique in that they require characters to be able to

reliably hit certain “benchmark” values on each roll to successfully complete a project. In designing an Exigent, it’s easiest to begin by determining what rating of artifact or sorcerous working you want that Exigent to be capable of reliably achieving, and then work backwards to ensure they’re capable of reaching the necessary benchmark value to do so. Remember that a character who’s heavily invested in that specific area of focus will be able to reliably roll fourteen dice before Charms (Attribute 5, Ability 5, an applicable specialty, exceptional equipment, and a one-point stunt), plus an automatic success from spending Willpower. You should use this maxed-out dice pool in calculating the expected value a character can reach — as with other Exalted, the Exigents must focus heavily in an area to reach the heights of what’s possible for them to attain.
