The most common way to structure a Charm set is to divide it up by Ability. For Solars, Dragon-Blooded, and other Ability-based Exalts, this means having Charms for all twenty-five Abilities, but that can be overwhelming. One useful approach is to limit an Exigent’s Charms to only five Abilities. This cuts down on how many trees an Exigent’s Charm set has, but it doesn’t limit their range of competency. Strawmaiden Janest, for instance, doesn’t have any combat Abilities; instead, her offensive Charms are concentrated in Athletics, with some in Awareness and Resistance. When you’re deciding what Ability (or Abilities) gets which competencies, there are two main factors to consider. The first is your Exigent’ themes. An Exigent of a bloody hand, a lesser god of murder, might have his offensive Charms concentrated in Investigation, with themes of both exacting vengeance on wrongdoers and pinpointing flaws in armor and fighting styles. The second consideration is how much conceptual or mechanical overlap there is between Abilities. Athletics and Ride are both used for movement actions, so a Chosen of the horse-god Hiparkes’ Ride Charms might enhance their movement on foot as well. Larceny and Stealth go hand in hand, and can almost always pick up each other’s competencies.

## Structuring Charm Sets

The first step in sketching an Exigent Charm set is to determine how it will be structured. In general, there are three main ways to divide Charm sets — Ability-based, Attribute-based, and Essence-based. No matter which of these you choose, be sure that each division has a high concept that helps to guide both flavor and mechanics for these Charms. The Dragon-Blooded, for example, filter each Ability through an elemental lens, while Solar Charms often emphasize a certain archetype or tactic: While all four Solar combat Abilities will help you be a better fighter, Brawl focuses on high damage at the expense of defense, Thrown emphasizes Join Battle rolls and stealth, Archery excels at decisive attacks over withering, and Melee is a generalist.

Making these decisions can be helpful in fleshing out concepts for an Ability’s Charm tree or organizing individual Charms you’ve written into a tree. If you decide that your Exigent of a saintly ice-god has defensive Charms in Integrity, and to focus on soak and Hardness-oriented defenses, you’ve put physicality and the body on the table for Integrity. From there, you might bring in the resilience to environmental hazards that typically appears in Survival, for meditating in the midst of blizzards — and maybe from there, controlling environmental hazards in a way that reflects their reverence for the Exigent’s virtue. Keep in mind that this isn’t an ironclad set of rules — it’s just one of many possible ways to approach structuring a Charm set.

EX3

### Attribute Charms

### Charm Compatibility

Attribute-based Charm sets can be more difficult to write, because Abilities often lend themselves to clearer high concepts, especially for Exigents. While you can give your Exigent Charms in all 9 Attributes (as we have done for the Architects), it’s also worth considering using a Charm set based on only 3 Caste Attributes. This can help give the Exigent a sense of focus, especially when creating a Charm set for a truly unique Exigent rather than one that encompasses a wider range of archetypes (again, as with the Architects).

Charms can generally only enhance actions or static values based on their associated Ability or Attribute unless otherwise indicated. When a Simple or Reflexive Lunar Charm creates an action, it must be rolled using that Charm’s Attribute unless specified. If a Charm enhances or creates an action or static value that’s not normally based on that Ability or Attribute, it is compatible with any Attribute or Ability normally associated with that action or value (e.g., Dexterity for a Strength Charm that enhances attacks).

Whichever you choose, Attribute-based Charm sets always further divide their Attributes into thematic trees. “Intelligence” is an overwhelmingly broad topic, so Lunars divide their Intelligence Charms among the themes of Knowledge, Mysticism, Crafting, Warfare, and Sorcery. Breaking the Attribute down into these themes helps to articulate that Attribute’s high concepts, and guides players to understanding the Exalt’s approach.

All Charms are compatible with Evocations by default. Attribute and Essence Charms are compatible with Martial Arts by default, although note that this compatibility will often need to be restricted at Terrestrial play for power level purposes, as with the Architects (p. XX).

When designing Attribute-based Charm trees, it’s especially important to consider the fact that these Charms are often more flexible than Ability-based ones and may need to have room to accommodate multiple character concepts. Lunars, for example, have many Appearance Charms that evoke fear and desire, which could all appeal to Lunar warriors, socialites, and mystics (albeit in very different ways).

### Essence Charms

Essence-based Charm sets work best when an Exigent has a progression of powers that couldn’t fit neatly within a single Ability or Attribute. The Puppeteer’s Charm set (p. XX), for example, is centered around her Charms based on puppetry and controlling animated puppets. Prerequisite Charms are key to Essencebased designs. They’re the sole source of structure for the Charm set, a logical or thematic progression from prerequisite to prerequisite, and are the sole determinator of how accessible a given Charm is. If you think your Exigent’s concept would work well with Ability or Attribute Charms, don’t use an Essencebased design just because; while it can be a useful design choice, it also comes with trade-offs. Ability- and Attribute-based trees provide a structure that helps funnel players toward the right Charms for their character concept; without them, players may have to read and internalize much more content than usual to make sure they’re building in the right direction.

## Charms and Theme

The themes of an individual Exigent inform all of their Charms, both individually and as a cohesive whole. However, rather than focusing in on a single theme or concept like “leadership,” “fire,” or “animals,” the best Charm sets reflect an expansive range of themes with room for nuance in how they’re expressed in Charms, with some themes given greater emphasis than others.

Think of a Charm set as a planet, with a core, mantle, and crust. The core of a Charm set encompasses the themes of the underlying Ability, Attribute, or Essencebased tree: An Exigent with Melee Charms is good at close combat, while one with Charisma Charms is good at influencing others. Core concepts are sometimes the least exciting, but they provide essential, workhorse effects that make an Exalt competitive in their chosen areas of specialization.

The mantle of a Charm set helps to explore that Exalt’s specific take on an Ability, Attribute, or theme. For a Solar, Blazing Solar Bolt extends her mastery of the sword by allowing her to use it at range; for a Lunar, Flesh-Sculpting Art allows her to extend her mastery of healing by changing a target’s flesh as if it were clay. For Exigents, these are where themes drawn from their divine patron’s purview and personality manifest themselves most strongly — and, for singular Exigents like the Puppeteer, themes drawn from their individual personality as well (p. XX).

EX3

Crust Charms are on the thematic fringe of an Exalt’s abilities, often stretching into metaphor. Wyld-Shaping Technique allows Solars to use their mastery of Lore to force the Wyld into the shape of Creation; Witch-Beast Ascendancy allows a Lunar to initiate her familiar into the secrets of sorcery itself. These Charms should be used sparingly and build from core and mantle Charms that slowly flesh out their associated theme. While rare, crust charms can often become iconic effects, especially because they tend to be flashy, desirable, and evocative.

## Anatomy of a Charm

Each Charm has a number of distinct mechanical components contained in its introductory description block. In addressing Charm design, we address these one by one, beginning with a Charm’s effect and moving through the other elements of the description block.

### Effect

The most important part of any Charm is what it actually does. In coming up with ideas for Charm effects, there are two main approaches: designing “top-down,” beginning with a Charm concept and finding mechanics to represent it, and designing “bottom-up,” beginning with the mechanic and then giving it a flavorful concept. Both approaches are important to designing a Charm set. “Top-down” designs often provide the most impressive and narratively impactful Charms that stand out within a Charm set. They begin with an idea for something cool you want your character to be able to do — “breathe a blast of venomous flame,” “detonate a zombie in an explosion of gore,” or “make someone trade places with their shadow.” Once you’ve done that, you’ll need to decide what mechanics that effect has. Referencing the effect index below (p. XX) or looking at other Charms that are close in function to your concept is a good way to find effects that you can either borrow wholesale or use as a jumping-off point for our own designs.

“Bottom-up” designs begin with the mechanical role they fulfill — “an attack that punishes high-soak enemies,” “a way to gain more Momentum in naval combat,” or “something to get rid of flurry penalties.” After that, you’ll need to decide the Charm’s flavor and what it represents in the game’s fiction when you use it. This doesn’t have to be hard — for many, the flavor is simply supernatural prowess in the Ability or Attribute they belong to. Bottom-up designs tend to be more common

### ORDER OF OPERATIONS

All calculations in Exalted follow the standard order of operations unless otherwise specified, with multiplication and division occurring prior to addition and subtraction.

than top-down ones, as they provide the crucial workhorse Charms — cheap, broadly applicable Charms that could reasonably be used every time you take the applicable action, like dice tricks. But while workhorse mechanics are one important role bottom-up designs play, that doesn’t mean they can’t also be impressive and powerful. Bottom-up Charms like Revolving Bow Discipline (Exalted, p. 259) can be just as flashy as any top-down design.

Once you have an idea for your Charm’s mechanic in mind, it will often be easiest to implement and balance that mechanic by comparing it to existing Charms and other effects. The ideal point of comparison would be one that’s for the same level of play as your Exigent, but you can also look at a stronger effect and limit or weaken it to bring it down to an appropriate level, or power up a weaker effect. This doesn’t mean that every design has to be a copy of an existing Charm, but it’s easiest to begin there, especially if you’re still new to designing Charms.

To assist in conceptualizing Charm effects, we’ve broken them down into the following groups. These aren’t meant to be rigid categories — they’re simply broad generalizations about different types of Charms in a way that provides some useful guidance for designing them. Enhancement Effects

An Enhancement effect lets you do something that you could already do, but better. This improvement could be purely numerical, adding bonus dice or enhancing the roll in various ways, but it could also be more qualitative, such as letting you complete an action in less time than it would normally take, or without some prerequisite that’s ordinarily necessary to successfully accomplish that action. Enhancement effects are typically Supplemental if they improve a rolled action, or Reflexive if they improve an application of a static value. To illustrate, of the Solar Charms in Exalted, about 40% are Enhancements; of the Charms in DragonBlooded, about 48% are Enhancements; and of the Charms in Lunars, about 36% are Enhancements.

EX3

Your own Charm sets don’t need to follow any of these allocations, but they provide a general guideline. Examples: Craftsman Needs No Tools (Exalted, p. 292), Hungry Tiger Technique (Exalted, p. 350), Masterful Performance Exercise (Exalted, p. 361), Seven Shadow Evasion (Exalted, p. 301). Enabler Effects

An Enabler effect lets you do something you normally couldn’t, no matter how many dice you roll. It’s a simple description, but a broad category: shooting phantasmal daggers from your eyes, creating a saltwater spring with poetry sad enough to make the earth weep, externalizing one of your Intimacies as a puissant god-beast, or more. Enabler effects are almost always Simple or Reflexive, although some Permanent Charms straddle the line between being an Enabler and being an Upgrade.

Of the Solar Charms in Exalted, about 33% are Enablers; of the Charms in Dragon-Blooded, about 40% are Enablers; and of the Charms in Lunars, about 30% are Enablers.

Examples: Blazing Solar Bolt (Exalted, p. 353), Essence-Lending Method (Exalted, p. 331), Glorious Solar Saber (Exalted, p. 350), Memory-Reweaving Discipline (Exalted, p. 363), Subtle Speech Method (Exalted, p. 323).

might provide a selection of options from a larger menu. The individual effects within a Utility Belt can themselves belong to any other category, but as a rule, they aren’t effects that would be sufficiently exciting or worthwhile as an entire Charm. Likewise, these individual effects are simpler than a standalone Charm, ensuring that the cognitive load of multiple effects in a single Charm purchase isn’t overwhelming. Utility Belt effects are often Permanent, although they can also be Simple or Reflexive Charms with ongoing durations. Of the Solar Charms in Exalted, the Charms in Dragon-Blooded, and the Charms in Lunars, about 2% are Utility Belt Charms.

Examples: Master Horseman’s Techniques (Exalted, p. 380), Salty Dog Method (Exalted, p. 386), Seasoned Criminal Method (Exalted, 315), Unsurpassed Hearing and Touch Discipline (Exalted, p. 272). Narrative Effects

Narrative effects are a rare subset of Enablers that allow the player to intervene in the story through dramatic editing, altering the present scene or the established setting in some way. This is still an expression of the character’s agency and skill — most often by revealing an action that the character has taken in the past, like a flashback in a heist movie, or through the introduce fact action (Exalted, p. 237), which is itself a Narrative effect.

Upgrade Effects

Upgrade Effects usually fall into one of two categories: either enhancing an existing Charm or acting as a permanent power-up for the Exalt. Charm-based upgrades increase a Charm’s power, remove restrictions, or expand options. Permanent power-ups provide an always-applicable benefit, like a bonus added on all rolls or extra health levels.

Of the Solar Charms in Exalted and the Charms in Lunars, about 1% are Narrative; of the Charms in Dragon-Blooded, fewer than 1% are Narrative.

Of the Solar Charms in Exalted, about 24% are Upgrades; of the Charms in Dragon-Blooded, about 9% are Upgrades; and of the Charms in Lunars, about 31% are Upgrades.

### Cost

Examples: Harmonious Academic Methodology (Exalted, p. 330), Invincible Fury of the Dawn (Exalted, p. 351), Ox-Body Technique (Exalted, p. 375), Searing Quicksilver Feint (Exalted, p. 299), Watchman’s Infallible Eye (Exalted, p. 311). Utility Belt Effects

Utility Belt effects bundle together smaller effects into a single Charm purchase. Some might provide all of these effects with just one purchase, while others

Examples: Dual Magnus Prana (Exalted, p. 292), GodKing’s Shrike (Exalted, p. 340), Infinitely-Efficient Register (Exalted, p. 288), Master Plan Meditation (Exalted, p. 318).

A Charm’s cost serves two main purposes. The straightforward function is as a resource cost necessary each time a character uses the Charm; the subtler function is limiting how often that Charm can be used, tied to the types of resources necessary to use it and the varying rates at which characters recover those resources. In finding the right cost for your Charms, the best approach is comparative — finding effects similar to the Charm that you’re designing in both function and rough power level, comparing their strengths and weaknesses to your Charm’s, and determining if your

EX3

Charm’s cost should vary from those of similar effects. As a rule of thumb, a specialized version of an existing effect — one that can only be applied under certain circumstances, as opposed to a universally applicable effect — should typically have a cost between 50% and 75% of the non-specialized effect’s cost, depending on how steeply the specialization limits the effect’s applicability.

Another important topic in costing Charms is the use of traits as variables in determining a Charm’s effect. A Charm that adds three dice on a certain kind of roll always adds three dice, but a Charm that adds (Integrity) dice can add anywhere from zero to five. In determining the value of a variable effect, start with the minimum value of the effect — e.g., three if the Charm requires a minimum Integrity 3 to learn — and take the average of the range of possible values between that minimum and the maximum. Note, however, that some traits are more valuable than others to a wide majority of character builds: player characters in general are far more likely to have high Dexterity or Wits than they are Perception, so an effect that adds (Dexterity) dice on an attack roll should cost more than one that adds (Perception) dice.

In discussing costs, we’ll refer to some resources being “worth” a certain amount of another to aid in this comparison, but this is only a rough guideline. Reallocating a Charm’s cost between different resources will have a significant impact on how often it can be used, and you should bear this in mind when making your comparisons. Motes

Motes are the most commonly used resource in Exalted and can be either spent to power instant-duration effects or committed to power an ongoing effect. When a character spends motes, they’re cleared from her mote pool, but she recovers them at the usual rate of five motes per combat round, or five motes per hour outside of combat. Committed motes are “tied up” in an ongoing effect and can’t be recovered until that effect ends. Note that committed motes aren’t recovered immediately at the effect’s end; the character must still wait and recover motes at the above rates. The ultimate comparison point for the value of spending a mote is the Excellency: one mote to add one bonus die to a given roll, with no restrictions. Most Charms that cost spent motes maintain this cost-to-value ratio — for instance, adding an automatic success is typically worth two motes — although specialized Charms may reduce it, as described above.

EX3

Five motes is an important cost threshold, especially in combat, for two reasons. Firstly, characters regain five motes each round in combat, meaning that a character can use a five-mote Charm every round in combat and never lose any motes, so long as she doesn’t use any other Charms. This isn’t a likely scenario in actual play but crossing the five-mote mark is what makes a character incur a long-term cost, and thus requires players to make decisions about which Charms they’ll use to enhance a certain action, and whether they’re willing to incur those long-term costs.

The other reason for the five-mote mark’s importance is that this is the threshold at which the expenditure causes an Exalted character’s anima to flare (Exalted, p. 175) if paid with peripheral motes (or personal motes, if the player wants their anima to flare). Anima is a double-edged sword: it can be used as a resource to pay some costs and is sometimes used as a variable in determining the strength of effects, but it also reveals a character’s Exalted nature and can impede stealth and disguise. The precise effect of this can vary greatly with a character’s concept and mechanical build. A Dragon-Blood with multiple Charms and Evocations that are strengthened by having a high anima will likely want to raise her anima as quickly as she can, while a Solar whose character build emphasizes stealth and who doesn’t have any Charms that grow stronger with her anima will avoid flaring as much as possible. Outside of combat, mote costs become more consequential, as it takes longer to recover them — a character could go through an entire scene of social influence in a prince’s court without ever recovering any of the motes she spends on her social Charms. However, some Charms are primarily intended to be used in situations that aren’t time-sensitive, where mote recovery isn’t as important. These primarily apply to extended rolls that occur over a long period of time, such as crafting, or Charms that are used during downtime. Their mote cost serves only to limit the total number of effects a character can afford to combine when enhancing their roll. The exact value of a mote cost becomes less important in this context; whether a crafting Charm costs ten motes or twenty is much less important than whether a combat Charm costs two motes or three. Committing motes is more onerous than spending them, as they can’t be recouped until the effect in question ends. There’s no easy benchmark of how much a committed mote will get you; comparing your design to similar effects will be the best way to pick a cost. The same five-mote mark considerations that apply to

spending motes also apply to committing them for any Charm that’s intended to be activated in same scene a character needs to use it, rather than being used in advance — typically Charms with a duration of one scene or less. In addition, committing motes effectively shrinks a character’s mote pool. While most characters can bear even a steep ten-mote commitment to a powerful Charm on top of a five-mote commitment to an artifact weapon, committing too many motes can leave a character without the motes they need on a roundto-round basis. You should avoid having too many Charms that require high-value commitments within the same field of activity to prevent players from potentially trapping themselves in this unfun situation by using too many ongoing Charms that they think are intended to be used together.

Willpower

Willpower costs are best used on powerful Charms that players aren’t meant to use on a consistent basis. Outside of combat, a character only recovers one Willpower per day, assuming she’s able to get a good night’s rest; in combat, characters have no reliable way of recovering Willpower unless they have Charms specifically for that purpose. Characters can also regain Willpower from two- or three-point stunts, from upholding Major or Defining Intimacies, and for accomplishing major story goals, but all of these are dependent on the Storyteller, rather than something that a player can proactively trigger. The difficulty of recovering Willpower, coupled with the limited amount that each player has, makes spending Willpower a more burdensome cost that requires greater consideration than spending motes.

Characters can spend one Willpower to add an automatic success to an (Attribute + Ability) roll, but most Charms with Willpower costs value Willpower more highly than that; one Willpower is worth roughly four motes. However, this resource cost is also cumulative with the restrictive effect of limited Willpower recovery; a Charm that costs five motes is much easier to use repeatedly on a consistent basis than one that costs one mote, one Willpower, even if the two costs are valued equally.

Willpower costs rarely go above one point, because players are often unwilling to invest so much in a single effect. As with mote costs, Willpower costs are less relevant on Charms that are used primarily during downtime, making them the best suited for higher Willpower costs, but even then, these costs should be reserved only for the most powerful of these effects.

EX3

that’s the typical amount of Initiative characters will reset to after landing a successful decisive attack or recovering from Initiative Crash, meaning characters will need to build additional Initiative after that before they can use those Charms without crashing themselves — and crashing yourself is almost never a good tactical decision. Initiative costs will rarely ever go higher than six Initiative.

### TIMING AND COSTS

A Charm that can be declared after a roll typically costs either four motes or one Willpower more than a comparable effect that must be declared before the roll, whether offensive or defensive. However, use caution in determining which effects a character can use after a roll, as being able to wait until after the outcome is certain before having to pay a Charm’s cost is a considerable advantage, and may render some effects inherently overpowered, such as making unblockable or undodgeable attacks, inflicting extremely large amounts of damage, severely punishing effects for losing the roll, or automatically succeeding regardless of the roll’s result. If in doubt about whether an effect should be allowed after the roll, check if any Charms designed for the same level of play allow for a comparable effect.

Anima

Anima levels are unique in that they’re generated by spending a different resource. Because a character can sustainably spend five motes each round in combat, they can also sustainably build one level of anima each round, although it’s also entirely possible to build a full three levels of anima in a single turn if a player’s willing to make that commitment. Additionally, characters can only have three levels of anima, so each level of anima spent represents a significant portion of a character’s total anima.

Initiative

Initiative is the core resource of Exalted’s combat system. Initiative costs should only be used on Charms meant for combat, and the Initiative component of a Charm’s cost is waived when it’s used outside of combat. They typically appear on combat effects that aren’t meant to be used on every attack or defense, requiring players to choose between using an effect and being able to use that Initiative to deal more decisive damage. Unlike other resources, the amount of Initiative a character will have at any given point is highly variable and fluctuates with withering and decisive attacks. Unlike motes, there’s no standard rate at which characters gain Initiative; a successful withering attack could yield only one to three Initiative if it’s reduced to minimum damage by soak, or it could yield upwards of fifteen with an Initiative Break. Initiative is generally valued at one mote per point. As an additional consideration, Charms with Initiative costs can’t be used while a character is crashed (and thus have the Perilous keyword by default). While it’s axiomatic that a cost can’t be paid if a character has none of the required resources, characters are much more likely to be crashed in combat than they are to run out of motes or Willpower. Another consideration is Initiative costs on Charms that enhance decisive attacks — each Initiative spent is one less die on the damage roll, while every three Initiative spent is effectively one less level of damage dealt. A Charm’s Initiative cost is typically less than its mote

cost. Three Initiative is a significant cost threshold, as

Anima costs are primarily but not exclusively used on Charms intended to be usable in combat. For non-combat Charms, anima costs should only be used when they reinforce the flavor of what the Charm is doing in the fiction of the game — for example, a Charm that lets an Exigent expel their anima banner as a wave of passion that rolls over a crowd.

Levels of anima are valued at one mote each, but like Willpower, this cost is also cumulative with the restrictive effect of having to spend five motes to gain one level of anima, as well as the Stealth penalties that accompany higher levels of anima.

Health Levels

Health level costs are relatively esoteric; they should be used only on Charms whose effect in the fiction of the game involves a character expending her life force to fuel her magic or suffering injuries as a result. All Exalted have a minimum of seven health levels, but any given character’s total can range as high as nearly thirty depending on the number of times they’ve bought Ox-Body Technique, their Exalt type, and their Stamina. Similarly, the rate at which health levels recover varies based on both the type of damage filling the health level and the wound penalty associated with the health level, ranging from one hour to five days (Exalted, p. 173). Healing magic can also complicate this further — a Solar can pay greatly in health level costs in a scene, then recover it all rapidly with a use of Body-Mending Meditation (Exalted, p. 375), while a Lunar can recover one health level on each turn with Halting the Scarlet Flow (Lunars, p. 256), potentially

EX3

letting them sustainably pay a non-aggravated health level cost in combat.

Note that Exigent experience, Solar experience, and the like can be used to pay experience point costs.

A health level is generally valued at five motes, although this cost is also combined with the limiting effect of potentially suffering wound penalties as a result of taking damage. The type of damage inflicted in paying a health level cost can largely be a matter of what best fits that Charm’s flavor but should take into consideration the healing magic available to an Exalt

type. For example, for Lunars, most Charms with

health level costs inflict aggravated damage, which their combat-time regeneration can’t heal; bashing or lethal health level costs are valued less than for Exalted who aren’t able to quickly and easily heal them.

Other Costs

While the above costs are the most commonly used, they aren’t an all-encompassing list. Some of Exalted’s systems have their own unique resources that can be used as a cost for Charms that interact with those systems. This is mostly commonly done with craft points (Exalted, p. 239), although others exist, such as naval combat’s Momentum (Exalted, p. 245). Because these resources are entirely dependent on an individual system, their valuation and pacing effect will vary between Exalt types based on how easy it is for that Exalt type to accrue the resource in question. For example, white craft points should be valued much more highly for Dragon-Blooded, who can only gain them by successfully crafting artifacts, than they are for Solars, who can easily reap large amounts of silver and gold points with Charms like Craftsman Needs No Tools and Supreme Perfection of Craft and then convert them to white points with Sublime Transference (Exalted, pp. 289, 292-293).

Limit

As a general rule, we avoid using Limit costs, in large part because many playgroups may opt not to use the Great Curse system due to its potentially unwanted impact on their game. While you’re free to do otherwise with your own design, you’ll need to take into account the general lack of effects that can serve as points of comparison. The main circumstance in which Limit costs would be used is for an Exigent or other Exalt type for whom the Limit mechanic is central to their Charm set, such as the apocryphal Umbral Exalted (p. XX).

As a cost, Limit is unusual because it is gained, rather than spent. A player can freely accumulate Limit until they reach ten points and enter Limit Break, at which point they must wait until the Limit Break ends to accrue any further Limit. In valuing Limit costs, you’ll need to take into consideration the ease with which an Exalt type can lose it — if they can only clear Limit through achieving legendary social goals, it might be comparable to Willpower, but if it’s easier for them to lose, its comparative value should decrease accordingly.

Experience Points

Experience point costs should be used extremely sparingly, if at all, as they are in short supply, and such costs compete with learning new Charms and increasing trait ratings. They should appear only on Charms whose use provides some significant, permanent benefit, such as Prophet-Uplifting Evocation (Exalted, p. 373), Spirit-Tied Pet (Exalted, p. 410), or WyldShaping Technique (Exalted, p. 335). Even then, such Charms usually waive the cost of their first use. If it’s possible that the benefit of such a Charm might be lost or become irrelevant to the game — e.g., if an empowered familiar is slain — a player should be refunded any experience points spent on it.

Additionally, an Exigent can have a unique resource that’s used only as a cost for their Charms, like DragonBlooded’s Elemental Aura (Dragon-Blooded, p. 162). In determining the value of such a resource, you can compare the rate at which it is gained or recovered, as well as any additional limiting effects it imposes, to those of the resources above. Given how complex Exalted already is, unique resources should be used sparingly to reinforce flavor and mechanical themes.

### Other Restrictions

A number of other mechanisms can be used to pace Charm use instead of or in addition to resource costs. Usage Limits

One of the most common restrictions is limitations on how often a character can use a specific Charm, such as once per scene or once per story, often coupled with a method to reset that Charm before the specified time period has elapsed.

Once per scene limitations most often appear on combat Charms that are extremely powerful, like Knockout Blow (Exalted, p. 278), Ruin-Abrasing Shrug (Exalted, p. 378) or Seven Shadow Evasion (Exalted, p. 301). They also appear on combat Charms that are especially cost efficient or that have no resource cost, such as Perfect Strike Discipline (Exalted, p. 351) or Supremacy of War Meditation (Exalted, p. 283).

EX3

Once per day limitations are used similarly, but for effects powerful enough that a character can’t necessarily use them every combat. They’re more common on Charms designed for Terrestrial play than those for Celestial play. Once per story limitations primarily appear on non-combat Charms with effects that are either extremely powerful and have an immediate and significant impact on the narrative, like Benediction of Archgenesis (Exalted, p. 480), God-King’s Shrike (Exalted, p. 340), or Infinitely-Efficient Register (Exalted, p. 288), or that provide an advantage that would be overwhelming even if limited to once being used once per day, such as Incalculable Flowing Mind (Exalted, p. 341), Steel Heart Stance (Exalted, p. 306), or Transcendent Hero’s Meditation (Exalted, p. 308). A slightly limited form of this restriction appears on Charms that can only be used against a given target once per story, such as Venomous Rumors Technique (Exalted, p. 402). These primarily appear on powerful social Charms and other effects that can inflicting debilitating conditions on enemies, ensuring that an enemy who successfully defends against it won’t simply be subjected to another use of it immediately. In all of these cases, a limited-use Charm’s reset condition ultimately determines of how often it can be used. Reset conditions can be tuned based on how difficult they are to achieve and whether they’re based on the player character’s actions or circumstances. For example, the Solar Charm Anointment of Miraculous Health (Exalted, p. 344) can only be used once per scene but can be reset by using a two-point stunt when treating a patient without the Charm. That’s relatively easy and the player can do so at their own direction. By contrast, Soul Voice (Exalted, p. 362) can only be reset when the Storyteller introduces a new complication to the scene. Other reset conditions can be outside the control of player and Storyteller alike to emphasize uncertainty and chance: Dragon-Blooded characters using Spine Shattering Bite (Exalted, p. 433) only reset the Charm when rolling four or more 10s on a decisive damage roll.

Resource Thresholds

Another method is to require a character to have a certain amount of a resource to use a Charm without requiring them to expend it. This is most often done with Initiative and anima levels, as these are the two resources that players can proactively accrue through their actions in combat or other scenes. Other examples include Dragon-Blooded Charms that require a character to be in an appropriate Elemental Aura, but that don’t expend the Aura.

Most Charms with an anima threshold trigger at bonfire anima, requiring a character to both spend at least fifteen motes and imposing sharp limitations on Stealth. While a character can sustainably reach bonfire after three rounds in combat, many fights don’t last that long, requiring a character to invest a significant number of motes to meet this threshold in time to use the relevant Charm. Lower anima thresholds are possible but less common; it’s easier on players if they only need to track whether they’re at bonfire or not to use their Charms. With regard to Initiative, a few specific thresholds are worth mentioning. 10 Initiative can potentially be reached with a single withering attack from base Initiative; 15 Initiative is a higher bar to meet, requiring a character to focus more effort on building Initiative and likely requiring multiple successful withering attacks without losing too much Initiative to enemies. 20 Initiative is both a very high bar and the point at which a character’s decisive attack can reliably kill most enemies in one hit; it’s a good threshold for the most powerful Charms that you want to be limited in their use.

Preparatory Actions

Actions represent perhaps the most important resource of all, because a character can only do so much at once. This is especially true in combat, where hostilities are often concluded within only a handful of rounds, making preparatory actions like aiming and shape sorcery actions a steep cost that demands a satisfying reward. Use preparatory actions sparingly, especially when they essentially force a character to do nothing — even if the reward is a powerful result, making a player twiddle their thumbs for a round is inherently discouraging.

### Type

Supplemental

Supplemental is the most basic Charm type, improving an action in some way — and thus, almost universally being Enhancements. In theory, Supplemental Charms only enhance rolled actions (like attacks or influence rolls) and actions for which no roll or value is relevant (such as aiming or full defense), while Charms that enhance static values like Resolve or Evasion are Reflexive. This division isn’t something you need to worry much about getting wrong, as it’s entirely superficial, with few mechanical implications, if any. Simple

A Simple Charm takes up a character’s entire turn, preventing them from taking other non-reflexive actions.

EX3

Likewise, Simple Charms can’t be used with Reflexive

Charms that allow a character to take an action.

Simple Charms fall into three main categories. The

first is Enhancement effects that provide an ongoing

benefit that typically lasts one scene or indefinitely.

For these Charms, the Simple type serves primarily as

a usage restriction, requiring a character to forgo their

turn to invoke their benefits. Keep in mind that many

combats will end in about three rounds, making giving

### TRANSPARENCY AND TIMING

Exalted’s system is built on the assumption of player-level transparency, with a handful of explicit excepExalted’s tions. Simply put, all players (including the Storyteller) must inform the others of what actions their characters take and what Charms or other effects they use, even though those players’ characters might be completely unaware of these details.

As a reminder, all Charms that affect a roll must be declared before the roll is made, even if their effect doesn’t take place until after the roll. For contested actions, all involved players must declare their Charms prior to the roll. Attackers must declare before defenders, but beyond that, there’s no set order in which players must declare actions or Charms. We recommend taking a casual approach and prioritizing getting Charms declared as quickly as possible.

If the order of declaration becomes tactically relevant and the players involved can’t agree on who declares first — e.g., if two characters act on the same tick, and both players want to declare their actions second so as to control whether or not the two characters clash — the Storyteller should flip a coin to determine who goes first. If more than two players are involved, each can roll a single die, with declaration proceeding from highest to lowest.

EX3

up a whole turn a significant cost. Try not to have too many of these Simple power-up Charms and assume that players probably won’t be able to use multiple such Charms in one scene. Weaker Enhancements can be made Reflexive Charms with ongoing duration, retaining the same effect but without the opportunity cost of giving up your action to use them. The second and third categories both have you make an action as part of using the Simple Charm — typically an attack or influence roll, but conceivably including any action. The second category is made up of Enhancement effects, providing a benefit to this action much like a Supplemental Charm. The difference is that characters can’t combine multiple such Simple Charms to enhance the same action. The third category is made up of Enabler and sometimes Narrative effects, letting you take an action that you normally wouldn’t be able to attempt at all.

Reflexive

Reflexive Charms encompass the broadest range of functions. The most basic Reflexive Charms are Enhancements that improve static values like Parry, Evasion, or Guile. They also include Charms that improve a roll or otherwise interact with it, but that are declared after the roll is made (note that these Charms must explicitly state they can be declared after the roll — by default, all Charms must be declared before the roll). The second category of Reflexive Charms is ongoing Enhancements, as described above in the Simple Charm section. The third category are Charms that allow you to take an action reflexively, such as attacking or aiming. Beyond these three categories, the Reflexive type is the one most suited to any miscellaneous effect that doesn’t neatly fit into any of the other types. If you ever find yourself unable to determine what a Charm’s type should be, Reflexive is almost always a safe choice. Permanent

Permanent Charms primarily provide a character with a permanent, always-active benefit, such as extra health levels or an improvement to one of their other Charms. Some Permanent Charms require a cost or surcharge to apply their benefits — some of these could in theory be Reflexive, but the distinction is generally unimportant.

### Duration

Duration is a relatively straightforward element of a Charm. We discuss some of the more common

durations, as well as some considerations specific to them.

Instant

An Instant-duration Charm is activated, does something, and then is done. Motes spent on an Instant-duration Charm aren’t committed. Note that an Instant-duration Charm can have effects that remain in place after its use for a specified duration, like the penalty inflicted by Joint-Wounding Attack (Exalted, p. 415); such Charms still don’t require a mote commitment, allowing one to potentially design ongoing Charms without one. Ticks

The tick is the smallest discrete unit of in-game time Exalted uses (Exalted, p. 192). One-tick duration is used primarily for Charms that either enhance multiple actions taken by a character (like both actions in a flurry) or defend against multiple actions taken by an opposing character (such as when an enemy uses a Charm to make multiple attacks against a character). We don’t recommend using multiple-tick durations; they’re unwieldy to track and offer little value to a designer compared to a one-round duration. Rounds

A Charm with a duration of measured in rounds lasts until the end of the appropriate round. As combat often lasts three rounds, you’ll rarely see Charms with a duration of more than one round; it’s better to use a scene-long duration for such effects.

Until Next Turn

A Charm with a duration of “until next turn” lasts until the next time the character who used it takes their turn in combat (Exalted, p. 192). The actual length of this varies based on when the character uses it and can change unpredictably if that character gains or loses significant amounts of Initiative, adjusting her place in turn order.

Scenes

Many if not most power-up Charms have a duration of one scene, meaning they’ll last for an entire fight or dramatic encounter. When in doubt, this is always a good default duration for lasting effects. Indefinite

Indefinite duration Charms remain in effect as long as Essence is committed. This duration is useful for Charms, especially power-up Charms, that require some kind of preparatory action, making the choice of uncommitting the motes invested in it more tactical since the character can’t automatically reactivate the Charm.

EX3

Days

Durations measured in days are similar to Indefinite duration, but more limited, requiring characters to renew it every so often if their player wants to keep that effect “on” all the time. It’s an especially common duration in Charms designed for Terrestrial play. Permanent

Permanent duration is exclusive to Charms with the Permanent type, and all Charms with the Permanent type have permanent duration. Note that if a Permanent Charm requires a mote cost, those motes aren’t committed unless the Charm specifies otherwise. Other Durations

Charms that supplement dramatic projects such as crafting, training, and bureaucracy sometimes have a duration of one project; this should be used carefully, because long and abstract durations can sometimes leave motes committed for multiple scenes or sessions, depending on timing.

### Keywords

The Four Main Combat Keywords

The Uniform, Dual, Decisive-only, and Withering-only keywords are used to identify what kind of attacks an offensive Charm can be applied to, or what kind of attacks a defensive Charm can be used against (for purposes of these keywords, Counterattack and Clash Charms are considered offensive).

Uniform Charms can be used with both withering and decisive attacks, with identical effects regardless of what kind of attack they’re enhancing or being used against.

Dual Charms can be used with both withering and decisive attacks but have either a different effect depending on which one they’re used with, or an additional effect when used with one or the other. Finally, Decisive-only Charms can only be used with decisive attacks, while Withering-only Charms can only be used with withering attacks. Note that gambits are decisive attacks. Clash

Clash Charms let you force an enemy attacking you into a clash (Exalted, p. 202) by reflexively making an attack against him. Some Charms may let you clash with other actions. You can’t use a Clash and a Counterattack Charm together against the same attack unless an effect specifically allows it. Note that

if a Charm lets you attack reflexively but doesn’t have the Clash keyword, like Peony Blossom Technique (Exalted, p. 346), it can’t be used to force a clash. Clash Charms can’t be used against Counterattack Charms. Counterattack

Counterattack Charms let you follow up an attack against yourself by attacking your attacker. Some Charms may let you counterattack with other actions. Unless the Charm specifies otherwise, this counterattack takes place after the enemy’s attack roll, but before their damage roll. You can’t use a Counterattack and a Clash Charm together against the same attack unless some effect specifically allows you to do so. Counterattack Charms can’t be used in response to Clash Charms or other Counterattack Charms. Perilous

Perilous Charms can’t be activated while a character is in Initiative Crash (Exalted, p. 193). This can be used to limit powerful Charms, and allows for tactical interaction, as a character can attempt to deny an enemy the use of his Perilous Charms by crashing him. Additionally, Charms with Initiative costs have the Perilous keyword by definition, as you can’t spend Initiative while at 0 or below. Note that ongoing Perilous Charms aren’t forcibly ended when a character is crashed unless they specifically state so — Perilous only prevents you from activating a Charm in the first place.

Mute

The Mute keyword lets an Exalt spend peripheral motes on a Charm without raising their anima. It appears primarily on Stealth Charms, Larceny Charms, and to a lesser extent on social Charms that benefit from being used subtly. Not all such Charms should be Mute, however — the tension between being able to use all one’s motes and needing to keep one’s anima hidden is an important part of the cost economy, and the lack of the Mute keyword can be used to balance powerful effects. Mute typically appears on Charms that cost 3+ motes; you should only add it to a 1-2 mote Charm if it needs that additional versatility to be worth a Charm purchase.

Psyche

While the Exalted and Creation’s other supernatural denizens are capable of incredible feats of eloquence, there’s a line between the words of a superhumanly gifted orator and a direct mental attack. The Psyche keyword identifies Charms that cross this line. Its application is based entirely on the concept and flavor of

EX3

the Charm in question. Manipulating a victim’s memory with Memory-Reweaving Discipline (Exalted, p. 363), embedding commands in a victim’s subconscious with Hypnotic Tongue Technique (Exalted, p. 372), or sorcerously manipulating a victim’s mind with spells like Corrupted Words (Exalted, p. 472) are all examples of Psyche effects. Functionally, the Psyche keyword identifies a Charm as being vulnerable to certain defensive effects such as Transcendent Hero’s Meditation (Exalted, p. 308).

Shaping

Shaping effects are any magic that transforms a character’s body, mind, soul, or the like. Which aspects of a character a shaping effect targets are denoted in a parenthetical — a Fair Folk’s petrifying gaze afflicts its victim’s body, while a Sidereal’s blessings and curses shape fate. Shaping effects can be defended against with magic like Destiny-Manifesting Method (Exalted, p. 304). The Shaping keyword is new to this book, but shaping effects aren’t. Those that appear in books released prior to Exigents typically specify that they are shaping effects in their text and are considered to have the Shaping keyword.

Written-only

This keyword denotes that a Charm that creates or enhances an influence roll is only compatible with written influence (Exalted, p. 221), not spoken influence. In Ability-based Charm sets, this typically applies only to Linguistics Charm, although Charms of other Abilities could interact with written influence. This keyword is more relevant in Attribute-based Charm sets, as Charisma and Manipulation Charms can enhance both written and spoken influence rolls by default.

Stackable

The Stackable keyword indicate Charms where multiple uses can stack their effects, like Joint-Wounding Attack (Exalted, p. 415), or Charms that lets a character sustain multiple active uses, like Indolent Official Charm (Exalted, p. 286).

Pilot

The Pilot keyword appears only on Charms that can enhance Sail rolls or that otherwise relate to travel by ship, requiring that a character be the captain or helmsman of a ship in order to use the Charm to enhance that ship’s movement or other actions. This is largely a matter of flavor — does your Charm make sense as something that can only be done while commanding or steering the ship? It also imposes a limit on how many characters can use their Pilot Charms to enhance a ship, preventing a group of Exalted from dividing up a set of Sail Charms amongst themselves and their mote pools, but this is rarely an important balance point. You don’t need to worry about Pilot breaking your designs. Aggravated

This keyword identifies Charms that can deal aggravated damage (Exalted, p. 173). It’s primarily just a label, although it’s possible that some effects might specifically enhance or defend against Aggravated Charms.

Bridge

The Bridge keyword appears on Charms that have an alternative set of prerequisite Charms, a certain number of unspecified Charms from a different trait or traits. (e.g., an Integrity Charm with any three War Charms as prerequisites). You don’t need to use the Bridge keyword to give a Charm such prerequisites, but it provides

### POISON, SICKNESS, CRIPPLING

Those familiar with Exalted Second Edition might wonder what’s become of the other keywords used to categorize various harmful effects. While they no longer exist as keywords, these effects are still a part of Exalted Third Edition.

Crippling effects most often appear in the form of crippling injuries (Exalted (Exalted,, p. 201) taken voluntarily by a player in place of suffering damage. Charms can also cause crippling effects when they inflict injuries whose debilitating effects go beyond the standard impairment of wound penalties, like Joint-Wounding Attack (Ex(Exalted,, p. 415), or directly impede the function of limbs or organs, like Crippling Pressure-Point Strike (Exalted (Exalted,, p. 428).

If a Bridge Charm isn’t Caste or Favored, player characters still receive the discount as long as all the prerequisite Charms they use are Caste or Favored. If a Bridge Charm already qualifies for the benefit, the number of Bridge prerequisites needed is halved, rounded up. (Solars with Supernal Integrity round this number down; other Exalted may have similar ways to do so). Additionally, a Charm used toward meeting a Bridge prerequisite can’t be used to learn other Bridge Charms; this restriction doesn’t apply to non-Bridge Charms.

Eclipse

The Eclipse keyword denotes non-Exalted Charms that can be learned through the Eclipse anima power or similar effects. The key consideration here is that Eclipse Charms shouldn’t compete with Solar Charms to fill particular roles, e.g., Defense penalty negator or decisive damage boost. Instead, it should be used for the most iconic and flavorful powers of a spirit, fae, or other supernatural being, like a field guardian’s power to make wheat grow to enormous sizes or rapidly reap a field or a storm mother’s power to call down lightning strikes (Exalted, pp. 513-514).

### Minimums

There’s a number of ways in which you can design effects that let an Exigent learn Eclipse Charms. You might design a Charm that grants access to a thematically appropriate subset of Eclipse Charms, or that lets an Exigent gain any Eclipse Charm through a thematically appropriate approach. An Exigent of the Wyldtainted god Xaos might be able to learn Eclipse Charms from the Fair Folk, as might a Chosen of Hallucination. A Chosen of the Hunt might be able to claim the Eclipse Charms of supernatural beings after tracking and subduing them, while a Chosen of the Market might be able to purchase access to a being’s Eclipse Charms. Of course, you can give an Exigent universal access to Eclipse Charms, like an Eclipse Caste Solar receives, but this should only be done when such a universal affinity for spirits and other supernatural beings reinforces the themes of that specific Exigent. Salient

The Salient keyword is no longer in use and should be considered deprecated. It appears only on two Solar Craft Charms, and the two are inconsistent in how it’s used. New Keywords

It’s not uncommon for Exalts to include their own custom keywords, especially when emphasizing their unique powers. The Dragon-Blooded have Aura, granting them additional benefits based on their current elemental alignment; Lunars have Protean, offering

When designing a new keyword, remember that their purpose is to centralize a commonly used mechanic in order to reduce repetition — the Puppeteer’s Entangled keyword emphasizes how important tagging enemies with the Entangled condition is to her fighting style. If a rule keeps popping up in many of your Charms, it’s worth considering whether it’s worth transforming into a keyword.

Essence Minimums

Essence minimums are primarily used to pace the growth of a character’s Charms over the course of a campaign.

Essence 1 Charms are available to player characters from the beginning of play. However, just because they’re the lowest Essence level doesn’t mean these Charms shouldn’t be powerful — to the contrary, Essence 1 Charms offer considerable power, both in the form of broadly applicable workhorse effects and in specialized effects that a character’s entire Charm build can be based around.

Essence 2 Charms provide only a small increase in power from Essence 1, focusing more on lateral progression and refining the options already available at Essence 1.

Essence 3 Charms see a significant increase in power from Essence 1 and 2. This will often be the highest Essence that player characters will attain, given that campaigns may not last long enough to progress beyond it. This power spike helps reinforce the feeling of growth and increasing power from character advancement even before player characters reach the highest levels of Essence.

Essence 4 Charms generally repeat the pattern seen at Essence 2, taking what’s available at Essence 3 and refining it or broadening its scope, utility, and complexity rather than simply increasing its power. Essence 5 Charms see another spike in power, though not as great as the one at Essence 3. For all practical purposes, this represents the maximum power the Exalted can attain, but reaching it in play requires a significant amount of real-world time — sometimes longer than a given campaign might last. Accordingly, while the level of power increases here, it’s not so drastic a jump as to

EX3

make a character who’s never able to progress beyond Essence 3 feel like they’re incomplete or diminished because of it.

The one major exception to the pattern above is Dragon-Blooded Charms. Because Dragon-Blooded begin at Essence 2, their Essence 1 and Essence 2 Charms cover effects that other Exalted have at Essence 1, their Essence 3 Charms cover effects that other Exalted have at Essence 2, and so on. It may be appropriate for you to deviate from the above pattern if it similarly serves some specific purpose for your overall design.

For guidance on how many Charms to include at each level of Essence, see p. XX.

Ability Minimums

While Essence minimums help to determine the power of a Charm’s effect, Ability minimums usually focus on reflecting how much specialization a character needs to qualify for the Charm: A Charm requiring Melee 2 is available to any Exalt who feels vaguely comfortable with a sword, while a Charm requiring Melee 5 is only meant for characters dramatically invested in armed combat.

EX3

• Ability 1 Charms are available to almost any character, and often represent universally applicable powers that all Exalts should have access to, such as Graceful Crane Stance and Ox-Body Technique.

• Ability 2 Charms often represent basic effects that need to be broadly available to characters. Spirit-Cutting Attack (Exalted, p. 354) is a key example — it’s something that many Exalted characters will pick up at some point in order to deal with dematerialized foes.

• Ability 3 Charms are the first point at which an Ability represents a real investment for the character. These Charms often include role-defining competencies, like Bulwark Stance (Exalted, 346), which offer the character significant power early on. • Ability 4 Charms expand on the specialization of Ability 3 Charms, offering greater power at the expense of further specialization. • Ability 5 Charms represent the bulk of many Ability-based Charm sets, especially for Charms that are deeper in their trees; this is because

once a Charm hits Ability 5, anything that builds off it inherits that same requirement. Ability minimums aren’t equally represented across all Essence levels. Charms that require Ability 1-2 are typically limited to Essence 1, with a few rare Ability 2 Charms at Essence 3; Essence 5 Charms almost universally require Ability 5.

• Attribute 2 Charms represent the lowest possible investment, making them accessible to any Exalt who hasn’t purposefully kept that Attribute below average.

• Attribute 3 Charms are roughly equivalent to an Ability minimum of 2 or 3, representing a relatively minor investment. • Attribute 4 Charms are roughly equivalent to an Ability minimum of 3 or 4 — enough to separate characters who are invested in this Attribute from dabblers.

• Attribute 5 Charms are used almost exclusively on high Essence Charms, allowing time for characters to grow into their main Attributes rather than requiring every player character to maximize their Attributes at character creation.

### Prerequisite Charms

Attribute minimums function like Ability minimums, gating access to a Charm based on specialization and archetype.

• Attribute 1 Charms are available to literally every character with no investment needed. These are very infrequently used, similar to Ability 1 Charms.

### ATTRIBUTE

### MINIMUM

One of the final ways to balance a Charm is through its prerequisites, creating trees that move from their roots (basic Charms with low requirements that anyone can learn relatively easily) to branches (high Essence, high requirement Charms that build on multiple earlier Charms to reward specialists). When designing an Exigent Charm tree, effects that every player character will need (including basic tools like penalty negators and the ability to interact with spirits) should come relatively early in a Charm tree, with no more than one or two prerequisite Charms.

If a Charm feels too powerful, you can give it more prerequisites, making it a reward for characters specializing in a certain direction. Be careful, though, to ensure that any prerequisites are useful and interesting in and of themselves: When using prerequisites as a balancing factor, it’s easy to invent speedbump Charms that do nothing other than soak up extra experience points.

### Not Recommended

As a final note, there are some effects that we actively recommend not including in your designs, either because they undermine major themes of Exalted in a way that diminishes the experience or because they have a strong tendency towards game-wrecking imbalance.

Resurrection

Exalted emphasizes the significance and impact of the choices made by the character and the consequences of those decisions. Death is one of the greatest consequences, and there is no such thing as true resurrection in Exalted’s setting. There may be things that come close, things that approximate resurrection — the existence of ghosts, sorcerous workings to manipulate the mechanisms of reincarnation, Liminal Exaltation

EX3

— but once someone is dead, the person that they were is gone, forever. No magic can undo this. Note that the prohibition against resurrection doesn’t extend to effects that let a character avoid death, or that make them agelessly immortal. Magic can reveal that a character’s seeming death was actually the destruction of a duplicate, grant a spirit’s ability to reform itself after its destruction if not slain with proper magic, or extend a character’s natural lifespan indefinitely. Such effects have their own balance considerations, and the thematic consideration of avoiding “boring” immortality (Exalted, p. 486), but those are separate concerns. Time Travel

Exalted’s emphasis on the importance of choices also means that time travel does not exist in the setting. Once you’ve made a mistake, you can’t travel into the past to take it back. In addition to this thematic significance, the system of Exalted isn’t designed in a way that handles time travel well. It takes thoughtful and careful design to create a roleplaying game that can make an enjoyable experience out of classic tropes of time travel fiction, such as traveling into the past to stop an enemy from being born, self-fulfilling time loops, and rewriting the present through small changes. Exalted simply wasn’t made for that purpose. Experience Points

Character progression in Exalted is based on the assumption that characters earn a flat five experience points each session, along with zero to four points of Solar Experience, Lunar Experience, or the like. Charms shouldn’t give characters additional experience points on top of this or allow them to use resources other than experience points to learn Charms, increase trait ratings, or the like. There are some Charms that violate this rule, such as Exegesis of the Distilled Form (Exalted, p. 291) and Flowing Mind Prana (Exalted, p. 331), but we don’t recommend doing the same. Similarly, Charms generally shouldn’t change the experience point cost of gaining or increasing a new trait. This is a guideline, rather than an absolute rule, as there is a very small design space where this can be done without causing balance issues. It primarily applies to the Craft Ability and its requirement that characters purchase multiple ratings in different Crafts. Supreme Celestial Focus (Exalted, p. 289) and Protean Creator Discipline (Lunars, p. 210) are both examples of exceptions to this guideline that don’t undermine the game’s balance. However, we don’t recommend using them as a basis of comparison for effects outside of Craft.

Copying Charms

As a general rule, the Exalted and other supernatural beings can’t learn the Charms of other types of supernatural beings — a Solar, for instance, can never learn Dragon-Blooded Charms. The Eclipse keyword is used to designate Charms that are exceptions to this rule; accordingly, Charms shouldn’t allow a character to learn non-Eclipse Charms belonging to another type of character.

There are a handful of effects that break this rule, like Carnal Spirit Rending (Exalted, p. 356) and Divine Mantle (Exalted, p. 310). We strongly recommend not following these precedents; they aren’t good comparisons for your own design. More Perfect Than Perfect

Some effects in Exalted are “perfect,” succeeding automatically despite all opposition. Seven Shadow Evasion (Exalted, p. 301) can perfectly dodge any attack; Eye of the Unconquered Sun (Exalted, p. 273) perfectly sees through all stealth and disguises. We don’t advise creating Charms to counter perfect effects, e.g., a perfect attack that even Seven Shadow Evasion can’t dodge. Such effects undermine the intent behind the design of perfect effects and would open the door to an endlessly escalating arms race of Charms for beating perfects, Charms for beating Charms for beating perfect effects, and so on. Morality

Exalted’s setting does not have any objectively ascertainable morality. This doesn’t mean that Exalted is amoral or morally nihilistic, or that it’s wrong to make claims about morality; rather, it emphasizes that morality is something that one must strive for in one’s actions and choices, something where there are no easy answers or certainties. The Unconquered Sun may be the Highest of Holies and the God of Virtue, but that doesn’t mean his judgments as to what’s good and what’s evil are any more definitive or correct than those of the Immaculate Order, the Yozis, or a mortal philosopher living in a wine barrel.

Thus, while the supernatural prowess of the Exalted can make them stronger, faster, and smarter than mortals, there is no Charm to make them morally better or to let them make wise decisions. Integrity Charms can make an Exalt’s commitment to their morals stronger, but they can’t ensure those morals are correct. Charms can’t tell you the morally right choice to make in a situation, or identify who is evil and who is good, because there is no objective basis for making those determinations.

EX3

## Putting It All Together: Designing an Example Charm

Speed Limit

Creation is a large world, and its size is narratively significant to the setting. The distance between two places impacts any story about war, diplomacy, commerce, or cultural exchange. While the Exalted can travel at incredible speeds, designing Charms that let them travel significantly faster than existing effects risks undermining the size of the setting, “shrinking” Creation for the player characters.

When looking for comparisons, note that Stormwind Rider (Exalted, p. 475) is an outlier, both in terms of how fast it lets characters travel at Essence 1 and how fast it lets characters in Terrestrial play travel. We don’t advise using it as a point of comparison for such effects unless one of the player characters already has it.

Putting It All Together:

Designing an Example Charm

June is designing a Chosen of Burning Feather, the goddess of intoxicants. They’ve decided that the Chosen of Intoxicants is intended for Terrestrial play, and has a limited Ability-based Charm set, with Charms in Integrity, Medicine, Occult, Presence, and Resistance. They’ve already written the following Charm, balancing it in comparison to Flexing the Emerald Claw (Exalted, p. 454) and Foe-Blinding Venom (Heirs to the Shogunate, p. 147):

#### Emptied Amphora Tragedy

Cost: 5m; Mins: Medicine 3, Essence 1

Type: Supplemental

Keywords: Decisive-only

Duration: Instant

Prerequisite Charms: Grape-Quickening Gesture

Wine-dark Essence swirls about the Chosen of Burning Feather’s weapon, imbuing her enemy’s blood with the heady potency of the finest brews. The Chosen’s decisive attack conveys a poison with Damage 1i/round (B in Crash), Duration (higher of Essence or 3) rounds, and a –2 penalty. If her target has an Intimacy that supports drinking, carousing, or hedonism, she adds its intensity to the poison’s duration, and her enemy’s (Stamina + Resistance) roll can’t lower the poison’s duration below that Intimacy’s

intensity. Conversely, if her target has an Intimacy of abstinence from drink or carnal pleasures, its intensity is subtracted from the poison’s duration.

Now, June wants to design a Charm to follow Emptied Amphora Tragedy that lets their Exigent expel the alcohol from an enemy’s system to inflict a debilitating hangover. Since Emptied Amphora Tragedy is Decisive-only, they want this follow-up Charm to be Withering-only.

There’s a number of different mechanical effects June could use to represent a magically inflicted hangover: dice penalties, losing Initiative or Willpower, taking small amounts of bashing damage that ignores Hardness, being forced to flurry each turn to be able to act, etc. Since using this Charm will mean giving up the Initiative damage and penalty inflicted by the purged poison, June decides to represent the dolorous hangover by inflicting an amount of bashing damage based on the rounds of poison expelled, as well as inflicting a crippling penalty for the rest of the scene. They write up this basic effect as follows:

When the Chosen of Burning Feather deals withering damage to an enemy suffering from the poison inflicted by Emptied Amphora Tragedy, she can purge that poison from his system to inflict one die of bashing damage, ignoring Hardness, for each round of the poison’s remaining duration. The damaged enemy also suffers a –2 penalty on all rolls until the scene ends, as a crippling effect. If there are bright lights or loud sounds present in the scene, the penalty rises to –3.

The most obvious type for this effect would be Supplemental, but it could also be Simple if making the withering attack was part of using the Charm, or Reflexive if it’s used after the damage roll. June decides to go with the straightforward option of Supplemental for now, with the option of changing it to Simple if there turn out to be any overpowered combinations between it and the Exigent’s other Simple combat Charms.

For duration, instant is the most likely choice, as this Charm enhances a single attack. However, because the crippling penalty lasts the entire scene, the Charm’s duration could be one scene. This would mean that the Exigent has to commit whatever the Charm’s mote cost ends up being for the entire scene, though, and

EX3

that seems both too steep for inflicting a penalty on one character and like something that might not be worth the extra bookkeeping.

For keywords, Withering-only is a given. June consults the list of keywords for any others it might need, but nothing else seems like a good fit — Mute and Perilous could both potentially be applied, but June doesn’t think this is the kind of covert effect that Mute would make sense on, nor does it seem like it needs the restriction of Perilous. Additionally, because successfully using Emptied Amphora Remorse will reset the Exigent’s Initiative, it leaves her wide open to be crashed before her next turn, potentially denying her the opportunity to use this hangover Charm altogether. That doesn’t seem like a fun scenario, given the amount of set up necessary to use this Charm, so Perilous is off the list. Finally, the Charm needs a cost and minimums. (Technically it also needs Prerequisite Charms, but June’s already decided that Emptied Amphora Tragedy is the prerequisite). To determine these, June looks at effects similar to theirs and suitable for Terrestrial

play: Fire Dragon style’s Essence-Igniting Nerve Strike (Dragon-Blooded, p. 294), White Veil style’s The Dragon Succumbs (Dragon-Blooded, p. 308), the Frost-Thorn Knuckles’ Blizzard Claw Swipe (Arms of the Chosen, p. 32), and the Ichneumon Blades’ Argent Brood Eruption (Lunars, p. 331).

While these effects all provide useful points of reference, Blizzard Claw Swipe, Essence-Igniting Nerve Strike, and The Dragon Succumbs are all Essence 3, while June would prefer this Charm to come after Emptied Amphora Tragedy at Essence 2, and Argent Brood Eruption requires the attack to crash an enemy to deal decisive damage, which June worries would make this too difficult to actually pull off in play, given the Charm already requires the Exigent to land a decisive attack and that the poison’s duration may expire before the enemy’s Initiative can be brought low enough to make crashing him feasible. As such, June decides to give their Charm a once-per-scene restriction in addition to its cost.

Putting it all together, June ends up with the following:

EX3

#### Dolorous Sobriety Strike

Cost: 4m, 1wp; Mins: Medicine 4, Essence 2

Type: Supplemental

Keywords: Withering-only

Duration: Instant

Prerequisite Charms: Emptied Amphora

Tragedy

### FULL EXCELLENCIES

When a Charm says it applies a full Excellency to a roll, it adds enough Charm dice to reach the rolling character’s dice limit. The character doesn’t actually need the Excellency for the Ability or Attribute in question to benefit. Likewise, when Charms like Rising Sun Slash require a character to use a full Excellency, they mean that she must have reached her dice limit by adding Charm dice and/or successes.

The Chosen of Burning Feather’s blows sends enemies reeling from their high-spirited carousing into the next day’s regrets.

If the Exigent deals withering damage to an enemy suffering from poison inflicted by Emptied Amphora Tragedy, she can purge that poison from his system to inflict an automatic level of bashing damage, ignoring Hardness, plus an additional level for every two rounds of the poison’s duration remaining, maximum (Essence) levels. The damaged enemy also suffers a –2 penalty on all rolls until the scene ends, as a crippling effect. If there are bright lights or loud sounds present in the scene, the penalty rises to –3.

Terrestrial (Withering): Overpowering Blockbuster Strike, Wrathful Winds Kiai (Dragon-Blooded, p. 289).

This Charm can only be used once per scene, unless reset by successfully landing a decisive attack enhanced with Emptied Amphora Tragedy that resets her Initiative and then building to Initiative 12+.

Bonuses on Attack Rolls

These Charms either add dice or successes on attack rolls, modify the roll beneficially, or weaken a target’s Defense.

### CHARMS AND DECISIVE ATTACKS

When a Charm tells you to make a decisive attack as part of using it, it means a damaging decisive attack, not a gambit, unless it specifically says otherwise. This typically comes up with Simple Charms and Charms that let you attack reflexively, like Counterattack and Clash Charms.

### AMBUSHES, CLARIFIED

When a character makes an ambush, the defending character is treated as having Defense 0 and can’t activate any Charms, Evocations, or the like in response to the attack unless those Charms explicitly state they can be used against ambushes or he uses magic like Reflex Sidestep Technique (Exalted, (Exalted, p.

299). He still receives the benefits of any Permanent Charms or Charms he’s already activated, but nothing can raise his effective Defense above 0 unless it explicitly works against ambushes.
